    Queue --> Worker[Worker]
    Worker -->|SETNX dedup_key TTL| DedupStore[(Redis Dedup Store)]
    DedupStore -->|key existed: skip| Worker
    DedupStore -->|key new: proceed| Process[Process Job]
    Process -->|crash before finish| Expire[Key expires via TTL]
    Expire -.->|reclaimable| Worker

title: Design an AI Agent Orchestration Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform that lets an LLM-based agent break a user's goal into a sequence of steps, call tools/APIs, and iterate based on results (an 'observe-plan-act' loop) until the goal is achieved.
stages.answer: Core loop: an orchestrator maintains agent state (goal, conversation history, available tools, results so far) and repeatedly prompts the LLM for the next action, which is either a tool call or a final answer. Each tool call is dispatched to a tool-execution layer (sandboxed, with a defined schema per tool), its result is appended to the agent's context, and the loop continues until the model signals completion or a step/time budget is exhausted. Persist state after every step so a crashed orchestrator process can resume rather than losing the whole run.

stages.prompt: Agents sometimes loop indefinitely (repeating similar failed tool calls) or run away with cost (each step is an LLM call). How do you bound this in production?
stages.answer: Enforce hard limits: a maximum step count, a wall-clock timeout, and a cost/token budget per run, with the orchestrator forcibly terminating and returning a partial result once any limit is hit. Detect repetition explicitly (e.g., hashing recent tool calls and flagging near-identical repeated calls) to short-circuit obvious loops before hitting the hard limit. Surface these guardrails as configurable per-use-case, since a customer-support agent might tolerate a much smaller budget than a long-running research agent.

stages.prompt: How do you make agent behavior debuggable and observable, given the LLM's reasoning isn't fully deterministic?
stages.answer: Log every step of the loop as a structured trace (prompt sent, model output, tool called with arguments, tool result, timestamp), not just the final answer, so a failed or weird run can be replayed and inspected step-by-step. Build a tracing UI that visualizes the full decision tree of a run, and track aggregate metrics (average steps per run, tool failure rate, cost per successful completion) to catch systemic issues rather than only debugging one run at a time.

    User[User Goal] --> Orchestrator[Agent Orchestrator]
    Orchestrator -->|prompt + context| LLM[LLM]
    LLM -->|next action| Orchestrator
    Orchestrator -->|tool call| ToolLayer[Sandboxed Tool Execution]
    ToolLayer -->|result| Orchestrator
    Orchestrator -->|persist each step| StateStore[(Agent State Store)]
    Orchestrator -->|trace| Tracing[Tracing/Observability]
    Orchestrator -->|final answer or budget exceeded| User

title: Design a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) System at Scale

stages.prompt: Design a RAG system that lets an LLM answer questions grounded in a large, frequently-updated corpus of internal company documents (millions of documents).
stages.answer: Ingestion pipeline: chunk documents into overlapping passages, compute embeddings for each chunk via an embedding model, and store them in a vector database alongside metadata (source, timestamp, permissions). At query time: embed the user's question, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks via approximate nearest neighbor search, optionally re-rank them with a cheaper cross-encoder for better precision, and inject the top results into the LLM's prompt alongside the question, instructing it to answer only from the provided context.

stages.prompt: Documents are updated and deleted constantly, and some documents are permission-restricted per user. How do you handle freshness and access control without re-embedding the whole corpus on every change?
stages.answer: For freshness, use incremental ingestion: only re-chunk and re-embed documents that changed since the last run (tracked via a content hash or last-modified timestamp), and delete/replace their vectors rather than rebuilding the whole index. For access control, store the document's permission metadata (ACLs, org/team ownership) alongside its vector, and filter retrieval results by the querying user's permissions at query time — never rely on the LLM to enforce access control after the fact, since a restricted chunk that reaches the prompt has already leaked.

stages.prompt: How do you evaluate and improve RAG answer quality over time, given it depends on both retrieval and generation?
stages.answer: Maintain a labeled evaluation set of representative questions with known-good answers/source documents, and track retrieval metrics (did the right chunk get retrieved, at what rank) separately from generation metrics (did the final answer correctly use the retrieved context, measured via an LLM-as-judge or human review) — since a bad answer could stem from either stage, and conflating them makes it hard to know what to fix. Continuously sample real production queries for review (with attention to low-confidence or user-flagged answers) to catch failure patterns the static eval set doesn't cover.

    Ingest --> VectorDB[(Vector DB\nembeddings + ACL metadata)]
    Query[User Question] -->|embed| Retriever[Retriever]
    Retriever --> VectorDB
    VectorDB -->|top-k chunks, filtered by user ACL| Rerank[Re-ranker]
    Rerank -->|top passages| LLM[LLM + Prompt]
    LLM --> Answer[Grounded Answer]
    Eval[Eval Set + Production Sampling] -.->|quality tracking| Retriever
    Eval -.-> LLM

title: Design an LLM Gateway (Multi-Provider API Router)

stages.prompt: Design a gateway that sits between your applications and multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models), giving a single unified API, handling authentication, and routing requests appropriately.
stages.answer: The gateway exposes one consistent API contract to internal callers, translating each request into the specific format each provider expects, and normalizing responses back to a common shape so callers don't need provider-specific code. It centrally manages API keys/credentials (callers never hold provider secrets directly), and can route a given request to a specific provider/model based on configuration (e.g., 'use Claude for this use case, GPT-4 for that one') without callers needing to know provider details.

stages.prompt: One provider starts returning errors/timeouts intermittently. How do you make the gateway resilient to a single provider's degradation without every calling application needing its own retry/fallback logic?
stages.answer: Implement automatic fallback at the gateway level: if the primary provider for a request fails or exceeds a latency threshold, retry against a configured secondary provider/model, transparent to the caller (though the caller may want to know which provider actually served the request, for cost/quality tracking). Use a circuit breaker per provider so that once failures cross a threshold, the gateway stops sending it traffic for a cooldown period rather than letting every request pay the cost of trying (and timing out against) a clearly-degraded provider.

stages.prompt: Different providers/models have very different costs. How do you add cost-aware routing and budget enforcement to the gateway?
stages.answer: Track cost per request (token counts × provider pricing) and aggregate it per team/application/API key, enforcing configurable budgets (hard cutoffs or soft alerts) centrally rather than requiring every team to track their own spend. For cost-aware routing, support policies like 'use a cheaper model for low-stakes requests, escalate to a more expensive model only if the cheaper one's output fails a quality check' — implementable as a simple two-tier routing rule or a more sophisticated classifier that predicts which requests need the expensive model.

title: Design a Prompt & Model Experimentation Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform that lets AI engineers version prompts, run them against multiple models, and compare results systematically before shipping a change to production.
stages.answer: Treat prompts as versioned artifacts (like code), stored with metadata (author, version history, associated eval set) rather than hardcoded in application code, so changes are tracked and reviewable. The platform runs a given prompt version against a defined evaluation set (representative test inputs with either known-good outputs or scoring criteria) across one or more candidate models, capturing outputs, latency, and cost for side-by-side comparison — turning 'does this new prompt work better' into a repeatable, comparable experiment rather than an engineer's subjective read of a few examples.

stages.prompt: How do you evaluate whether a new prompt version is actually better, especially for open-ended generation tasks where there's no single 'correct' answer?
stages.answer: Combine multiple evaluation signals rather than relying on one: automated checks where possible (format validity, keyword/constraint presence), an LLM-as-judge scoring outputs against a rubric for more subjective quality dimensions, and periodic human review of a sample, especially before a significant change ships. Track these scores per prompt version over time so a regression is visible immediately, and require a new version to meet or beat the current production version on the eval set before it's eligible for rollout.

stages.prompt: How do you safely roll out a new prompt/model version to production once it passes evaluation?
stages.answer: Use the same staged-rollout discipline as any risky production change: deploy the new version to a small percentage of live traffic (or a shadow mode comparing its output against production without acting on it), monitor real-world signals (user feedback, regeneration rate, downstream task success) alongside the offline eval scores, and progressively increase traffic only if those signals hold up — keeping the previous version as an instant rollback target rather than assuming the offline eval fully predicts production behavior.

title: Design an AI Agent Tool-Calling Sandbox

stages.prompt: Your AI agent platform lets agents execute arbitrary code or shell commands as one of their available tools (e.g., a coding assistant that runs code to verify its own output). Design the execution environment for this.
stages.answer: Execute all agent-requested code in an isolated, ephemeral sandbox (a container or microVM) with no network access by default, strict CPU/memory/time limits, and a filesystem that's wiped after each execution — never execute untrusted, model-generated code directly on a shared host. Return only the captured stdout/stderr/exit code (and any explicitly-produced output files, if that's a supported capability) back to the agent, treating the sandbox as a fully disposable, isolated unit of work per execution.

stages.prompt: A malicious or buggy agent-generated script attempts to consume unbounded resources or exfiltrate data over the network. What specific isolation guarantees does your sandbox design need?
stages.answer: Resource limits enforced at the container/VM level (CPU quota, memory limit, disk quota, execution timeout) that the sandboxed process cannot override from inside; no network access by default (or a tightly allow-listed egress if some tools genuinely need it, e.g., a specific API), preventing data exfiltration or the sandbox being used to attack other systems; and no access to the host filesystem or other tenants' sandboxes, using per-execution ephemeral environments rather than a shared long-lived sandbox that could accumulate state or cross-contaminate between users.

stages.prompt: How do you scale this sandbox execution layer to handle many concurrent agent sessions cost-effectively, given spinning up a fresh container per execution has overhead?
stages.answer: Maintain a warm pool of pre-initialized sandbox containers/microVMs ready to be assigned to an incoming execution request, avoiding cold-start latency on every call, and recycle (destroy and replace) a sandbox after each use rather than reusing it for a different session, to preserve isolation guarantees. Autoscale the pool size based on observed concurrent demand, and consider lightweight microVM technology (like Firecracker) specifically because it offers strong isolation with much faster startup and lower overhead than full VMs, which matters a lot at the request volumes agentic tool use can generate.

title: Design a Vector Database

stages.prompt: Design the core of a vector database that stores high-dimensional embedding vectors and answers approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries efficiently at scale (hundreds of millions of vectors).
stages.answer: Exact nearest-neighbor search (comparing a query against every stored vector) doesn't scale past a modest number of vectors, so the core design decision is an approximate index structure — common choices include HNSW (a navigable graph structure enabling fast approximate search) or IVF (partitioning vectors into clusters and only searching relevant clusters). Store vectors plus associated metadata (for filtered search) together, and expose an API for insert/delete/query-by-similarity with a configurable top-k and similarity metric (cosine, dot product, Euclidean).

stages.prompt: The dataset grows to a scale where the index no longer fits in memory on a single machine. How do you shard the vector index across multiple machines while keeping query latency low?
stages.answer: Partition vectors across shards (e.g., by a hash of the vector's ID, or via a learned/clustering-based partitioning that groups similar vectors together to reduce cross-shard queries), and for each query, fan out to all shards in parallel, retrieve each shard's local top-k candidates, then merge and re-rank the combined candidate set at a coordinator layer to produce the final top-k. This scatter-gather pattern trades some coordination overhead for the ability to scale index size roughly linearly with the number of shards.

stages.prompt: How do you support metadata filtering (e.g., 'find similar vectors, but only among documents the user has access to') without it destroying query performance?
stages.answer: Pure post-filtering (retrieve top-k by similarity, then discard results that don't match the filter) breaks down when the filter excludes most candidates, since you might discard almost everything and return too few results. Better approaches include pre-filtering within the ANN search itself (index structures that support filtered traversal, only exploring the subset of the graph/clusters matching the filter), or maintaining separate indexes per common filter dimension (e.g., per-tenant indexes) when filter cardinality is low and predictable enough to make this practical — the right choice depends on filter selectivity and cardinality, which is worth stating explicitly as the deciding factor.

    Coordinator --> Shard3[(Shard 3)]

title: Design a Feature Store for Machine Learning

stages.prompt: Design a feature store that lets multiple ML teams define, compute, and reuse features consistently for both offline model training and low-latency online inference.
stages.answer: Separate the feature store into an offline store (a data warehouse holding historical feature values for training, computed via batch pipelines over historical data) and an online store (a low-latency key-value store like Redis holding the current value of each feature for real-time inference lookups), fed by the same feature definitions/transformation logic so training and serving stay consistent. Features are registered with metadata (owner, description, computation logic, freshness SLA) in a central registry so teams can discover and reuse existing features rather than each team recomputing similar features independently.

stages.prompt: A model trained on features computed one way in the offline store performs worse in production than expected. Investigation reveals the online store's feature computation logic had subtly drifted from the offline version. How do you prevent this class of bug (training-serving skew)?
stages.answer: Define feature transformation logic once, in a single shared codebase/specification, and generate both the offline batch computation and the online real-time computation from that same definition, rather than maintaining two independently-written implementations that can drift apart. Add automated consistency checks that periodically compare offline and online feature values for the same entity at the same point in time and alert on unexpected divergence, catching skew early rather than only discovering it via a degraded model.

stages.prompt: How do you handle features that require expensive computation (e.g., aggregating a user's last 90 days of transactions) while still meeting a strict low-latency requirement for online inference?
stages.answer: Precompute and continuously update expensive aggregate features in the background (via a streaming pipeline that incrementally updates the aggregate as new events arrive, rather than recomputing from scratch on every request) and simply look up the current precomputed value at inference time — turning an expensive computation into a fast key-value read. This requires the feature store's online layer to support this streaming-update pattern, not just static batch refreshes, for features that need to reflect very recent activity.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    RawData[(Raw Event Data)] --> BatchPipeline[Batch Feature Pipeline]
    RawData --> StreamPipeline[Streaming Feature Pipeline]
    BatchPipeline --> OfflineStore[(Offline Store - training)]
    StreamPipeline --> OnlineStore[(Online Store - Redis, serving)]
    Registry[(Feature Registry\nshared definitions)] --> BatchPipeline
    Registry --> StreamPipeline
    Training[Model Training] --> OfflineStore
    Inference[Online Inference] --> OnlineStore
    Consistency[Consistency Checker] -.-> OfflineStore
    Consistency -.-> OnlineStore

title: Design an ML Training Pipeline Orchestrator

stages.prompt: Design a system that lets ML teams define multi-step training pipelines (data prep → training → evaluation → registration) as reusable, schedulable workflows across a shared GPU cluster.
stages.answer: Model each pipeline as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of steps with explicit dependencies, where each step runs as a containerized job with its own resource requirements; the orchestrator (similar to Airflow or Kubeflow Pipelines) schedules each step once its dependencies complete, tracks artifacts (datasets, model checkpoints) passed between steps, and retries failed steps without re-running the whole pipeline.

stages.prompt: Multiple teams submit pipelines competing for the same limited GPU pool. How do you allocate fairly while still letting high-priority jobs run promptly?
stages.answer: Use a priority-aware job scheduler (queueing with priority classes and fair-share quotas per team) rather than pure first-come-first-served, so no single team can monopolize the cluster, while allowing an explicit high-priority lane for urgent jobs. Support preemption carefully — checkpointing long-running jobs so a preempted job can resume rather than losing all progress — since preemption without checkpointing just shifts unfairness onto whichever job gets evicted.

stages.prompt: How do you ensure a training run is fully reproducible months later when someone asks 'how was this exact model produced'?
stages.answer: Version and record everything the pipeline used: exact code commit, dataset version/hash, hyperparameters, environment/dependency versions, and random seeds, all tied to the resulting model artifact in a metadata store — so reproducing a run means replaying a fully-specified recipe rather than reconstructing it from memory or scattered notes.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Submit[Pipeline Submission - DAG] --> Scheduler[Priority-aware Scheduler]
    Scheduler --> GPUPool[(Shared GPU Cluster)]
    GPUPool --> DataPrep[Data Prep Step] --> Train[Training Step] --> Eval[Eval Step] --> Registry[(Model Registry)]
    Metadata[(Run Metadata Store\ncode, data, params, seeds)] -.-> Train
    Metadata -.-> Registry

title: Design a Real-Time Fraud Detection System

stages.prompt: Design a system that scores every transaction for fraud risk in under 100ms, combining rule-based checks with an ML model.
stages.answer: On each transaction, fetch precomputed features from a low-latency feature store (user's recent transaction history, velocity checks, device fingerprint), run fast deterministic rules first (hard blocks like a known-stolen card), then score the transaction with the ML model, combining rule outputs and model score into a final decision (allow, block, or flag for manual review) — all within the latency budget by keeping every step in the hot path fast and precomputed rather than doing heavy computation synchronously.

stages.prompt: Fraud patterns evolve constantly as fraudsters adapt. How do you keep the model effective without constantly manual-retraining?
stages.answer: Continuously monitor model performance against labeled outcomes (confirmed fraud/chargebacks arriving with a delay), track drift in key feature distributions, and set up automated or frequent scheduled retraining on recent data so the model incorporates new patterns rather than staying frozen at its original training snapshot; combine this with a fast-path rule system that can react to a newly-identified fraud pattern within hours, since model retraining is inherently slower than the pace fraud rings can adapt.

stages.prompt: A legitimate transaction gets incorrectly blocked (a false positive), frustrating a real customer. How do you balance fraud prevention against this cost?
stages.answer: Treat the decision threshold as a tunable business tradeoff, not a fixed technical constant — track both false-positive rate (blocked legitimate transactions) and false-negative rate (missed fraud) explicitly, and let risk/product stakeholders set the threshold based on the actual cost of each error type for the business. For borderline-confidence transactions, route to manual review or a secondary verification step (like a confirmation code) instead of a binary allow/block, reducing the cost of uncertainty.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Txn[Incoming Transaction] --> Rules[Fast Rule Checks]
    Txn --> FeatureStore[(Feature Store)]
    FeatureStore --> Model[ML Fraud Model]
    Rules --> Decision[Decision Engine]
    Model --> Decision
    Decision -->|allow/block/review| Response[Response < 100ms]
    Outcomes[(Confirmed Fraud Outcomes)] -.->|retraining loop| Model

title: Design a Content Moderation System

stages.prompt: Design a system that moderates user-generated content (text, images) at the scale of millions of posts per day, using a mix of automated ML classifiers and human review.
stages.answer: Run every piece of content through fast automated classifiers first (text toxicity models, image classifiers for policy violations), which handle the large majority of clearly-fine or clearly-violating content automatically; route only ambiguous/borderline cases (classifier confidence in a middle range) to a human review queue, since human review doesn't scale to full volume and shouldn't need to.

stages.prompt: Human moderators need to review flagged content quickly, and moderator wellbeing matters given exposure to disturbing content. How do you design the review workflow?
stages.answer: Prioritize the review queue by severity and virality (a violating post gaining rapid traction needs faster review than a low-visibility one), and route content to appropriately-trained moderator pools by content category. For moderator wellbeing, apply protective measures like blurring/graying disturbing images by default until explicitly revealed, capping continuous exposure time, and providing support resources — this is a real operational design concern, not just a technical afterthought.

stages.prompt: How do you handle appeals when a user disputes a moderation decision, and how do you improve the system based on those appeals?
stages.answer: Provide a clear appeals path where a different reviewer (not the original one) re-examines contested decisions, and track appeal outcomes (overturned vs. upheld) as a direct quality signal on both the automated classifiers and individual human reviewers. Feed overturned decisions back into classifier retraining and reviewer calibration/training, since a high overturn rate on a specific violation category is a strong signal that classifier or policy needs adjustment.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Content[User-Generated Content] --> Classifier[Automated Classifiers]
    Classifier -->|clear violation| AutoAction[Automated Removal]
    Classifier -->|clearly fine| Publish[Published]
    Classifier -->|ambiguous| ReviewQueue[Human Review Queue\nprioritized by severity]
    ReviewQueue --> Moderator[Moderator Decision]
    Moderator -->|disputed| Appeals[Appeals - different reviewer]
    Appeals -.->|feedback| Classifier

title: Design an AI Customer Support Chatbot Platform

stages.prompt: Design a chatbot platform that resolves common customer support queries automatically via an LLM, escalating to a human agent when needed, integrated with a company's knowledge base and ticketing system.
stages.answer: Use a RAG-based architecture where the LLM answers grounded in the company's actual knowledge base/documentation (to reduce hallucination on policy-sensitive answers like refunds), with tool-calling access to backend systems (order lookup, account status) so it can act on real data, not just describe generic steps. Define clear escalation triggers — the model expressing low confidence, the user explicitly asking for a human, detecting frustration/repeated re-asks, or the query falling into a category defined as always-human (like account security issues) — handing off to a human agent with full conversation context rather than making the user repeat themselves.

stages.prompt: How do you prevent the bot from confidently giving wrong answers on things like refund policy or account actions, where being wrong has real cost?
stages.answer: For high-stakes categories, require the model's answer to be strictly grounded in retrieved policy documents (not generated from general knowledge), and add a verification step for any action with real consequences (like issuing a refund) — the bot can propose the action, but final execution goes through an explicit confirmation or a business-rule engine that validates it's actually permitted, rather than trusting the LLM's own judgment on policy compliance.

stages.prompt: How do you measure and improve the bot's performance over time?
stages.answer: Track resolution rate (queries fully handled without escalation), customer satisfaction on bot-handled conversations, and escalation reasons (which reveal gaps in knowledge base coverage or capability) as core metrics. Use escalated conversations as a direct feedback loop — reviewing why the bot couldn't handle them and using that to expand knowledge base coverage or refine prompts/tools, treating escalations as the most valuable signal for where the system needs improvement.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    User[Customer] --> Bot[LLM Support Bot]
    Bot --> KB[(Knowledge Base - RAG)]
    Bot --> Tools[Backend Tools\norder lookup, account status]
    Bot -->|low confidence/frustration/policy| Escalation[Escalate to Human Agent]
    Escalation -->|with full context| Agent[Human Agent]
    Agent -.->|resolution feedback| KB

title: Design a Multi-Agent Collaboration System

stages.prompt: Design a system where multiple specialized AI agents (e.g., a researcher agent, a coder agent, a reviewer agent) collaborate on a complex task, each with different tools and capabilities.
stages.answer: Use an orchestrating 'manager' agent (or a defined workflow) that decomposes the overall task into subtasks and assigns each to the appropriate specialized agent based on required capability, collecting each agent's output and feeding relevant results to downstream agents (e.g., coder agent's output goes to the reviewer agent). Each specialized agent operates with its own narrower tool access and context, which both improves focus (a coder agent doesn't need the same tools as a researcher) and limits blast radius if one agent misbehaves.

stages.prompt: Agents can get stuck disagreeing (e.g., reviewer agent keeps rejecting coder agent's output) or the overall task never converges. How do you handle this?
stages.answer: Set explicit iteration limits on inter-agent back-and-forth (e.g., max 3 review-revise cycles) before escalating to a human or accepting the current best result rather than looping indefinitely, mirroring the same runaway-loop protection a single agent needs. Log the full multi-agent conversation/handoff trace so a stuck collaboration is debuggable — was the reviewer being overly strict, was the coder not addressing feedback, etc. — rather than just seeing a timeout with no insight into why.

stages.prompt: How do you keep costs manageable when a complex task might involve many agents each making multiple LLM calls?
stages.answer: Set a total budget (cost/token/step count) for the entire multi-agent task, not just per individual agent, so the orchestrator can track cumulative spend and terminate gracefully with a partial result if the budget is exhausted. Use cheaper/smaller models for simpler subtasks (a routing or formatting step doesn't need your most expensive model) and reserve the most capable model for the specific subtasks that actually need it, similar to cost-aware routing in a single-agent system.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Task[Complex Task] --> Manager[Manager Agent]
    Manager -->|subtask| Researcher[Researcher Agent]
    Manager -->|subtask| Coder[Coder Agent]
    Coder --> Reviewer[Reviewer Agent]
    Reviewer -->|feedback loop, max N cycles| Coder
    Researcher --> Manager
    Reviewer -->|approved| Manager
    Manager -->|budget exceeded or complete| Result[Final Result]

title: Design an LLM Fine-Tuning Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform that lets ML teams fine-tune LLMs on custom datasets without each team building their own training infrastructure from scratch.
stages.answer: Provide a managed pipeline: teams upload/point to a training dataset (validated against a required format), select a base model and fine-tuning method (full fine-tune vs. parameter-efficient methods like LoRA), and submit a job that the platform schedules onto the GPU cluster, handling distributed training setup, checkpointing, and logging automatically so teams don't need deep infrastructure expertise to fine-tune a model.

stages.prompt: How do you validate a dataset before an expensive training run starts, to avoid wasting GPU-hours on a run that fails or produces a bad model due to bad data?
stages.answer: Run automated pre-flight checks on the dataset before scheduling the expensive job: format/schema validation, checking for empty or malformed examples, flagging extreme outliers (like the abnormally long examples that caused the NaN-loss incident discussed earlier), and computing basic statistics (size, class balance for classification tasks) for the team to sanity-check. Catching data problems in a fast pre-flight check is far cheaper than discovering them hours into a multi-GPU training run.

stages.prompt: How do you let teams evaluate whether their fine-tuned model is actually better than the base model before deploying it?
stages.answer: Require (or strongly encourage) an evaluation step as part of the standard pipeline, not an optional afterthought — running the fine-tuned model against a held-out test set and against the base model on the same set, surfacing a clear comparison (task-specific metrics, and ideally a sample of side-by-side outputs) so the team makes an informed decision rather than assuming fine-tuning helped just because training completed without errors.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Dataset[Training Dataset] --> Preflight[Pre-flight Validation]
    Preflight -->|passes| Scheduler[Training Job Scheduler]
    Scheduler --> GPUCluster[(GPU Cluster)]
    GPUCluster --> Checkpoint[(Checkpoints)]
    Checkpoint --> Eval[Evaluation vs Base Model]
    Eval -->|comparison report| Team[ML Team Decision]
    Team -->|approved| ModelRegistry[(Model Registry)]

title: Design a Semantic Search Engine

stages.prompt: Design a search engine that returns results based on semantic meaning rather than exact keyword matching, for a large product catalog (tens of millions of items).
stages.answer: Compute embeddings for each product (from its title, description, and possibly image) and store them in a vector index for approximate nearest-neighbor search; at query time, embed the search query and retrieve the most semantically similar products. Combine this with traditional keyword/inverted-index search (a hybrid approach) since pure semantic search alone can sometimes miss exact-match intent (a user searching an exact model number wants that exact item, not just something semantically similar).

stages.prompt: Users complain that semantic search sometimes returns results that are thematically related but not what they actually wanted, while keyword search sometimes misses relevant results phrased differently. How do you combine both approaches?
stages.answer: Run both semantic and keyword search in parallel for each query and merge/re-rank the combined candidate results using a ranking model that considers signals from both (semantic similarity score, keyword match score, plus business signals like popularity/conversion rate) — rather than picking one approach exclusively, hybrid retrieval generally outperforms either alone since they have complementary strengths and failure modes.

stages.prompt: How do you keep the semantic index up to date as products are added, updated, and removed continuously, without periodic full reindexing becoming a bottleneck?
stages.answer: Support incremental updates to the vector index (insert new product embeddings, update changed ones, remove discontinued ones) as products change, rather than only supporting full rebuilds — most modern ANN index structures support this, though some (depending on implementation) periodically benefit from a background reindex/compaction pass to maintain search quality/performance as the index accumulates changes over time, which should be run without blocking live queries.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Query[Search Query] --> Semantic[Semantic Search\nvector similarity]
    Query --> Keyword[Keyword Search\ninverted index]
    Semantic --> Merge[Hybrid Re-ranker]
    Keyword --> Merge
    Merge -->|business signals: popularity, conversion| Results[Ranked Results]
    ProductUpdates[Product Catalog Updates] -->|incremental| VectorIndex[(Vector Index)]
    ProductUpdates -->|incremental| InvertedIndex[(Inverted Index)]

title: Design an AI Code Review Assistant Backend

stages.prompt: Design a backend service that automatically reviews pull requests using an LLM, posting comments on potential bugs, style issues, and suggestions, integrated with GitHub/GitLab.
stages.answer: On a PR event (webhook), fetch the diff plus relevant surrounding context (the full changed files, and potentially related files/definitions the diff references), construct a prompt asking the model to review for specific categories (bugs, security issues, style, missed edge cases), and post the model's findings as PR comments via the platform's API, ideally anchored to the specific lines they concern rather than one generic top-level comment.

stages.prompt: Large PRs can exceed the model's context window, and reviewing every single line with equal depth is wasteful. How do you handle this?
stages.answer: Chunk large diffs into logical units (per-file, or per-function where changes are large) and review each chunk with enough surrounding context to be useful, rather than trying to fit an entire large PR into one prompt. Prioritize review depth by risk — changes to core business logic, security-sensitive code, or complex control flow deserve more scrutiny than a documentation-only or purely mechanical formatting change, which can be reviewed lightly or skipped entirely.

stages.prompt: Developers start ignoring the bot's comments because too many are low-value nitpicks or false positives. How do you fix this?
stages.answer: Track comment-level feedback (did the developer act on it, dismiss it, or react negatively) as a direct signal, and use it to tune what categories of finding get surfaced — if a specific type of comment is consistently dismissed, either fix the underlying prompt/logic causing false positives or stop surfacing that category by default. Consider a severity threshold (only post comments above a certain confidence/importance bar) rather than surfacing every possible observation, since comment volume and perceived value are in direct tension — a bot that comments on everything trains developers to ignore it entirely.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    PR[Pull Request Event] --> Fetch[Fetch Diff + Context]
    Fetch --> Chunker[Chunk by File/Function\nprioritize by risk]
    Chunker --> LLM[LLM Review]
    LLM --> Comments[Post PR Comments]
    Comments -->|developer reaction| Feedback[(Feedback Tracking)]
    Feedback -.->|tune prompts/thresholds| LLM

title: Design a Model Evaluation & Benchmarking Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform that lets ML teams run standardized evaluations of models (both internal fine-tuned models and third-party LLMs) across multiple benchmark datasets and custom eval sets.
stages.answer: Provide a registry of evaluation datasets/tasks (both standard public benchmarks and internal custom eval sets per use case) and a runner that executes a given model against a chosen set of evaluations, computing standardized metrics (accuracy, task-specific scores, latency, cost) and storing results tied to the exact model version evaluated, so results are comparable across models and over time rather than one-off, unreproducible numbers.

stages.prompt: Some evaluations require subjective judgment (is this generated response actually good) rather than exact-match scoring. How do you handle these at scale?
stages.answer: Use an LLM-as-judge approach for subjective evaluations — a strong model scores candidate outputs against a defined rubric — while explicitly tracking the judge's own reliability (periodically validating LLM-judge scores against human judgment on a sample, since the judge itself can be biased or miscalibrated). For evaluations where correctness really matters, blend automated LLM-judge scoring with periodic human review rather than relying on either exclusively.

stages.prompt: How do you prevent benchmark results from becoming misleading over time (e.g., a model being implicitly 'trained to the test' or benchmarks becoming stale)?
stages.answer: Rotate and periodically refresh eval sets (especially ones derived from public data that might leak into future training corpora), keep some held-out evaluation data that's never shared or exposed even internally, and track real-world production performance alongside benchmark scores as a check — since a model that looks great on a static benchmark but underperforms in actual usage is a signal the benchmark has stopped being representative.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Model[Model Under Test] --> Runner[Eval Runner]
    BenchmarkRegistry[(Benchmark & Eval Set Registry)] --> Runner
    Runner --> AutoScoring[Automated Scoring\nexact-match, metrics]
    Runner --> LLMJudge[LLM-as-Judge Scoring]
    LLMJudge -.->|periodic validation| HumanReview[Human Review Sample]
    AutoScoring --> ResultsDB[(Results DB - versioned)]
    LLMJudge --> ResultsDB

title: Design a Real-Time Personalization Engine for E-commerce

stages.prompt: Design a personalization engine that adapts product recommendations and page layout in real time based on a user's current browsing session, not just their historical profile.
stages.answer: Maintain a real-time session feature store capturing the user's in-session actions (items viewed, searched, added to cart) as they happen, and combine these fast-changing session signals with the user's longer-term historical profile (from a separate, less frequently updated store) at recommendation time — session signals capture immediate intent (what are they shopping for right now) that a purely historical profile would miss entirely.

stages.prompt: Computing fresh personalized recommendations on every single page view for every user is expensive. How do you make this performant at scale?
stages.answer: Separate candidate generation (a broader, cheaper retrieval step that narrows the full catalog to a manageable candidate set, often precomputable or cacheable per user-segment) from final ranking (a more expensive, personalized model applied only to the smaller candidate set at request time) — this candidate-generation-then-ranking pattern is the standard way large-scale recommendation systems balance personalization quality against the cost of scoring millions of items per request.

stages.prompt: How do you measure whether the personalization engine is actually improving business outcomes, not just producing recommendations that look reasonable?
stages.answer: Run controlled A/B tests comparing the personalized experience against a baseline (non-personalized or previous version), measuring actual business metrics (click-through rate, conversion rate, revenue per session) rather than only offline ranking metrics, since offline metrics can look good while failing to move real user behavior. Continuously experiment with variations (different ranking models, different candidate generation strategies) rather than treating the system as 'done' once launched.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    SessionEvents[Real-time Session Events] --> SessionStore[(Session Feature Store)]
    HistoryStore[(Historical Profile Store)] --> Candidates[Candidate Generation]
    SessionStore --> Candidates
    Candidates -->|smaller candidate set| Ranker[Personalized Ranking Model]
    Ranker --> Recommendations[Recommendations Shown]
    Recommendations -->|A/B test| Metrics[(Business Metrics)]
    Metrics -.->|iterate| Ranker

title: Design an Agentic Workflow Automation Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform (like Zapier, but AI-powered) that lets non-technical users describe an automation goal in natural language, and the system builds and executes a workflow connecting multiple third-party services (email, calendar, CRM, etc.).
stages.answer: An LLM interprets the user's natural-language goal and, using a defined set of available integrations (each exposed as a structured tool with a schema, similar to an agent's tool-calling setup), proposes a workflow (a sequence or DAG of steps connecting specific services) for the user to review and approve before it's activated — critically, showing the user exactly what the automation will do rather than only executing silently, since users need to trust and verify automations that will run unattended, potentially affecting real data (sending emails, modifying records).

stages.prompt: An activated workflow runs unattended and something in one of the connected services changes unexpectedly (an API schema change, a permission revoked). How do you handle failures gracefully?
stages.answer: Each workflow run should be monitored with clear failure detection (a step's API call fails, returns unexpected data, or the workflow doesn't complete as expected), triggering a notification to the workflow's owner rather than failing silently — a broken automation nobody knows about is often worse than no automation at all, since the user may be relying on it. Support automatic retries with backoff for transient failures, but distinguish those from failures needing human attention (like a revoked permission) that retrying won't fix.

stages.prompt: How do you let users trust that an AI-generated workflow won't do something harmful or unintended (e.g., accidentally emailing the wrong list, or looping and sending duplicate actions)?
stages.answer: Require explicit user review/approval of the generated workflow before activation (never auto-activate an AI-proposed workflow silently), provide a dry-run/test mode that simulates the workflow against sample data without taking real actions, and build in safety rails for high-consequence actions specifically (like requiring extra confirmation for anything that sends communications to an external list, or capping the volume of actions a single workflow run can take to prevent a runaway loop from, say, sending thousands of duplicate emails).

diagram:
flowchart TD
    User[User Goal - natural language] --> LLM[LLM Workflow Builder]
    Integrations[(Available Integrations)] --> LLM
    LLM -->|proposed workflow| Review[User Review & Approval]
    Review -->|approved| Activated[Activated Workflow]
    Activated --> Execution[Scheduled/Triggered Execution]
    Execution -->|failure| Notify[Notify Owner]
    Execution -->|safety rail: action cap| Execution

title: Design a Voice Assistant Backend

stages.prompt: Design the backend for a voice assistant: audio comes in from a device, and a spoken response comes back, with the assistant able to answer questions and take actions.
stages.answer: Pipeline: speech-to-text (STT) converts incoming audio to text, the text is processed by an LLM (with tool-calling access for actions like setting a timer or checking weather), and the response text is converted back to audio via text-to-speech (TTS) and streamed back to the device. Streaming is important at each stage (partial STT results, streaming LLM tokens, streaming TTS audio) to minimize perceived latency — waiting for each stage to fully complete before starting the next would make the assistant feel sluggish.

stages.prompt: Users expect near-instant responses, but the full STT → LLM → TTS pipeline has real latency at each step. How do you minimize perceived response time?
stages.answer: Start TTS generation on the first portion of the LLM's streamed output before the full response is generated, rather than waiting for the complete text response (this pipelining across all three stages, not just within one, is what actually gets end-to-end latency down). Use a lightweight, fast wake-word/intent-detection model to start warming up the pipeline (or determine no LLM call is even needed, e.g., for a simple 'what time is it') before the full STT transcription completes, for very common quick interactions.

stages.prompt: How do you handle ambiguous or misheard voice input (STT errors, background noise) gracefully rather than the assistant confidently acting on a wrong transcription?
stages.answer: Surface STT confidence scores to the downstream LLM step so genuinely uncertain transcriptions can trigger a clarifying question ('did you mean...') rather than confidently acting on a likely-wrong interpretation, especially before taking any consequential action (like sending a message or making a purchase) based on voice input. For high-stakes actions specifically, consider requiring an explicit confirmation step regardless of transcription confidence, since voice input error rates are inherently higher than typed input.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Audio[Incoming Audio] --> STT[Speech-to-Text\nstreaming]
    STT --> LLM[LLM + Tool Calling\nstreaming]
    LLM --> TTS[Text-to-Speech\nstreaming]
    TTS --> Device[Audio Response to Device]
    STT -->|low confidence| Clarify[Clarifying Question]
    LLM -->|high-stakes action| Confirm[Explicit Confirmation]

title: Design an LLM Observability & Tracing Platform

stages.prompt: Design a platform that gives engineers visibility into what's happening inside LLM-powered applications in production — every prompt sent, every response, every tool call, latency, and cost — across potentially many different applications and teams.
stages.answer: Instrument every LLM call and tool call as a structured trace event (input, output, latency, token counts, cost, associated metadata like user/session/application), collected centrally and organized so a full multi-step interaction (like an agent's whole run) can be viewed as a connected trace, not just isolated individual calls. Provide both an aggregate dashboard view (cost/latency/error trends across an application) and a detailed per-trace drill-down view for debugging specific problematic interactions.

stages.prompt: The volume of trace data across many high-traffic LLM applications is enormous. How do you keep this observable without the observability system itself becoming prohibitively expensive?
stages.answer: Apply sampling for full-detail trace storage (store 100% of aggregate metrics, but only a representative sample — or all traces matching specific criteria like errors, low-confidence outputs, or user-flagged interactions — at full detail), similar to how general distributed tracing systems handle high-volume services. Use tiered retention (recent traces fully queryable, older traces compressed/archived), since most debugging happens on recent data.

stages.prompt: How do you help teams actually find problems in this data, rather than just having it available to search through reactively?
stages.answer: Build automated alerting on key signals (latency/cost/error-rate anomalies, spikes in a specific failure pattern, degradation in an automated quality score if one is tracked) so teams are proactively notified rather than needing to manually dig through dashboards to notice a problem. Support flagging/annotation so a human reviewer (or a user's own feedback signal, like a thumbs-down) can mark specific traces as notable, building a curated set of interesting failure cases over time that's more useful than an undifferentiated firehose of raw trace data.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    App[LLM Application] -->|structured trace events| Collector[Trace Collector]
    Collector --> Sampling[Sampling: full detail on errors/flagged, sampled otherwise]
    Sampling --> TraceStore[(Trace Store - tiered retention)]
    TraceStore --> Dashboard[Aggregate Dashboard]
    TraceStore --> Drilldown[Per-trace Drilldown]
    TraceStore --> Alerting[Automated Alerting]
    Alerting -->|anomaly detected| Team[Engineering Team]

title: Design a Payment Gateway

stages.prompt: Design a payment gateway (like Stripe) that processes card payments on behalf of merchants, integrating with card networks and banks.
stages.answer: Core flow: a merchant's checkout submits payment details to the gateway (ideally via a tokenized/hosted field so raw card data never touches the merchant's own servers, for PCI compliance), the gateway validates and routes the request to the appropriate card network/acquiring bank, receives an authorization response, and returns a result to the merchant — with the actual fund settlement happening asynchronously afterward. Idempotency keys on every payment request are essential so a network retry from the merchant's side can't accidentally double-charge a customer.

stages.prompt: A payment can fail partway through (authorized but the merchant's confirmation call times out) — how do you avoid inconsistent state between the gateway and the merchant's system?
stages.answer: Design the API around idempotent, retryable operations and webhooks: the gateway is the source of truth for payment state, and the merchant polls or (more commonly) receives webhook notifications of state changes rather than relying solely on the synchronous response to a request that might have timed out despite succeeding server-side. This means a merchant can always ask 'what actually happened to this payment' and get an authoritative answer, rather than being stuck not knowing if a timed-out request actually went through.

stages.prompt: How do you handle the strict compliance and security requirements (PCI-DSS) around handling card data at this scale?
stages.answer: Minimize the scope of systems that ever touch raw card data — use tokenization aggressively (card details are exchanged once for a token, and all subsequent operations use the token, never the raw card number again) and isolate the few systems that must handle raw card data into a tightly audited, separately secured environment, since PCI compliance scope and cost scale with how many systems touch sensitive card data directly.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Merchant[Merchant Checkout] -->|tokenized card data| Gateway[Payment Gateway]
    Gateway -->|idempotency key| AuthEngine[Authorization Engine]
    AuthEngine --> CardNetwork[Card Network / Acquiring Bank]
    CardNetwork --> AuthEngine
    AuthEngine --> Gateway
    Gateway -->|webhook: payment state change| Merchant
    Gateway --> Settlement[(Async Settlement)]

title: Design a Multi-Tenant SaaS Platform

stages.prompt: Design the data architecture for a B2B SaaS product serving thousands of customer organizations (tenants), where each tenant's data must be strictly isolated from others.
stages.answer: Common approaches, in increasing order of isolation (and cost): shared database with a tenant_id column on every table plus row-level filtering enforced in every query (cheapest, but isolation depends entirely on application code never forgetting the filter); shared database with per-tenant schemas; or fully separate databases per tenant (strongest isolation, most operational overhead). The right choice depends on tenant count and size — thousands of small tenants usually favor the shared-database-with-tenant_id approach with strict enforcement, while a smaller number of large enterprise tenants can justify per-tenant databases.

stages.prompt: With the shared-database-plus-tenant_id approach, a single missed WHERE clause in application code could leak one tenant's data to another. How do you make this class of bug much harder to introduce?
stages.answer: Don't rely purely on developer discipline to always include the tenant filter — enforce it structurally, e.g., via database row-level security policies that make the database itself refuse to return rows outside the current tenant context regardless of the query, or via a data-access layer that automatically injects the tenant filter into every query so it's structurally impossible to forget rather than a convention to remember.

stages.prompt: One large enterprise tenant's heavy usage is causing noisy-neighbor performance problems for other tenants on the same shared infrastructure. How do you address this?
stages.answer: Apply per-tenant resource quotas/rate limits so one tenant's load can't degrade others' experience, and consider tiered infrastructure — moving especially large or performance-sensitive tenants to dedicated infrastructure (a dedicated database, or a separate deployment) while smaller tenants share a pool, which is a common pattern once a SaaS platform has a wide range of tenant sizes.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    TenantA[Tenant A Request] --> App[Application Layer]
    TenantB[Tenant B Request] --> App
    App -->|tenant context enforced| DataLayer[Data Access Layer\nauto tenant_id filter]
    DataLayer --> SharedDB[(Shared DB - RLS enforced)]
    LargeTenant[Large Enterprise Tenant] --> DedicatedDB[(Dedicated DB)]
    Quotas[Per-tenant Quotas] -.-> App

title: Design a Feature Flag System

stages.prompt: Design a feature flag system that lets engineering teams toggle features on/off and roll out changes to a percentage of users, without deploying new code.
stages.answer: Store flag definitions (name, targeting rules — percentage rollout, specific user/org allowlists, environment) in a central config service; application instances fetch and cache the current flag configuration (via SDK, polling, or a push/streaming update), evaluating each flag locally per-request against the current user's context (user ID, org, attributes) without a network call on every single evaluation, since flag checks need to be very low-latency and shouldn't add a request-time dependency on the flag service being available.

stages.prompt: How does a flag change (e.g., turning off a feature during an incident) reach thousands of already-running application instances quickly?
stages.answer: Use a push-based update mechanism (a streaming connection, or a pub/sub notification triggering a re-fetch) rather than relying only on periodic polling, so a change can propagate within seconds rather than waiting for the next poll interval — this matters a lot for the 'emergency kill switch' use case, where an engineer needs to disable a broken feature immediately during an incident, not after an unpredictable polling delay.

stages.prompt: How do you prevent feature flags from accumulating indefinitely and turning the codebase into an unmaintainable maze of conditional logic?
stages.answer: Treat flags as having an explicit lifecycle, not permanent fixtures: track flag age and usage, flag ones that have been at 100% rollout (or 0%) for a long time as candidates for cleanup, and make removing a fully-rolled-out flag's conditional code a standard, expected follow-up task rather than an optional nice-to-have that never happens — the system itself can help by surfacing stale flags rather than leaving this entirely to developer memory.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Engineer[Engineer] -->|update flag| ConfigService[(Flag Config Service)]
    ConfigService -->|push update| App1[App Instance]
    ConfigService -->|push update| App2[App Instance]
    App1 -->|local evaluation, no per-request network call| Decision1[Flag Decision]
    ConfigService --> StaleFlagReport[Stale Flag Report]
    StaleFlagReport -.-> Engineer

title: Design an API Gateway

stages.prompt: Design an API gateway that sits in front of dozens of backend microservices, providing a single entry point that handles routing, authentication, and rate limiting.
stages.answer: The gateway terminates incoming requests, authenticates/authorizes them (validating tokens, potentially calling an auth service), applies rate limiting per client, then routes the request to the appropriate backend service based on path/host rules, aggregating or transforming responses if needed before returning to the client. Centralizing these cross-cutting concerns at the gateway means individual backend services don't each need to reimplement authentication and rate limiting themselves.

stages.prompt: The gateway becomes a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck for the entire platform's traffic. How do you address this?
stages.answer: Run the gateway as a horizontally-scaled, stateless fleet behind a load balancer (never a single instance), so no individual gateway node is a single point of failure, and any node can handle any request. Keep the gateway's own logic fast and mostly stateless (caching auth decisions briefly rather than calling the auth service on every single request, for instance) since it sits on the critical path of every request to every backend service, making its own latency and reliability a multiplier on the whole platform's.

stages.prompt: How do you handle a scenario where one backend service becomes slow or starts failing, without it dragging down the gateway's ability to serve requests to other, healthy services?
stages.answer: Apply per-backend-service circuit breakers and timeouts at the gateway, so a struggling service gets isolated (requests to it fail fast rather than piling up waiting) without consuming gateway resources (connections, threads) that are needed to serve requests to unrelated, healthy backend services — this bulkhead-style isolation is exactly the kind of cross-cutting resilience concern that's valuable to centralize at the gateway layer rather than reimplementing per-client.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Client --> LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> GW1[Gateway Node]
    LB --> GW2[Gateway Node]
    GW1 -->|authn/authz, rate limit| AuthService[Auth Service]
    GW1 -->|route + circuit breaker| ServiceA[Backend Service A]
    GW1 -->|route + circuit breaker| ServiceB[Backend Service B - degraded]
    ServiceB -.->|isolated failure| GW1

title: Design a Distributed Tracing System

stages.prompt: Design a distributed tracing system (like Jaeger or Zipkin) that lets engineers follow a single request's path across dozens of microservices to debug latency and errors.
stages.answer: Each service, on receiving a request, propagates a trace context (a trace ID shared across the whole request, plus a span ID for that service's specific unit of work) to any downstream calls it makes, and reports completed spans (service name, operation, start/end time, tags, parent span ID) to a central collector. The collector assembles spans sharing a trace ID into a full trace, letting a UI reconstruct the entire request's call tree with per-hop timing, showing exactly where time was spent or where an error originated.

stages.prompt: Instrumenting every service call adds overhead, and at high request volume, storing every single trace in full detail is expensive. How do you manage this?
stages.answer: Apply sampling — commonly head-based sampling (deciding whether to trace a request at its very start, propagating that decision through the whole call chain so it's consistent) at some percentage of overall traffic, often combined with always sampling traces that hit an error or exceed a latency threshold (since those are exactly the traces engineers most want to inspect), rather than uniformly sampling and potentially missing the interesting cases.

stages.prompt: How do you make it easy for an engineer debugging a specific slow request (reported by a user) to find that exact trace among millions collected?
stages.answer: Ensure the trace ID is surfaced somewhere accessible for correlation — logged alongside application logs, included in error responses/support tooling, or exposed in internal debugging headers — so a specific user-reported incident can be tied back to its exact trace ID and looked up directly, rather than an engineer having to search through traces by approximate time and hope they find the right one.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Client --> ServiceA[Service A - span 1]
    ServiceA -->|propagate trace ID| ServiceB[Service B - span 2]
    ServiceB -->|propagate trace ID| ServiceC[Service C - span 3]
    ServiceA -->|report span| Collector[Trace Collector]
    ServiceB -->|report span| Collector
    ServiceC -->|report span| Collector
    Collector --> TraceStore[(Trace Store)]
    TraceStore --> UI[Trace Visualization UI]

title: Design a Secrets Management System

stages.prompt: Design a secrets management system (like HashiCorp Vault) that lets applications securely retrieve credentials (database passwords, API keys) without secrets being hardcoded or checked into source control.
stages.answer: Secrets are stored encrypted at rest in a central service; applications authenticate to the secrets service (via a machine identity mechanism like a cloud IAM role or a short-lived token, not a hardcoded credential — that would just move the secret-management problem, not solve it) and request the specific secrets they need at startup or runtime, rather than having secrets baked into config files or container images.

stages.prompt: A secret is compromised (leaked in a log, or a credential is suspected stolen). How does the system support fast, safe rotation?
stages.answer: Design for short-lived, frequently-rotated credentials as the default rather than long-lived static secrets — dynamically generating database credentials with a short TTL per application instance, for example, means a leaked credential is only useful for a limited window automatically, and full rotation (immediately invalidating everything) is a supported, tested operation, not a manual scramble across dozens of services that all hardcoded the old value.

stages.prompt: How do you audit and control which applications/teams can access which secrets, given a leak or misuse needs to be traceable?
stages.answer: Enforce fine-grained access policies (which identity can read which specific secret path) and log every single secret access (who/what accessed which secret, when) immutably, so any suspected leak or misuse can be traced to its exact source. Treat the secrets service's own access logs as a first-class security signal to monitor, not just an operational nicety — an unusual access pattern (a service reading a secret it's never accessed before) is a meaningful anomaly worth alerting on.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    App[Application] -->|machine identity auth| SecretsService[Secrets Service]
    SecretsService -->|short-lived credential| App
    SecretsService --> EncryptedStore[(Encrypted Secret Store)]
    SecretsService --> AuditLog[(Immutable Access Audit Log)]
    SecretsService -->|dynamic generation| DB[(Database)]
    Policy[Access Policies] -.-> SecretsService

title: Design a CI/CD Pipeline System

stages.prompt: Design a CI/CD system that automatically builds, tests, and deploys code changes across many repositories and teams, at a company with hundreds of engineers.
stages.answer: On a code push/PR event, trigger a pipeline (defined as config alongside the code) consisting of stages (build, test, security scan, deploy) executed on a scalable pool of build workers/runners, with each stage's pass/fail gating progression to the next; deployments to production typically require the pipeline to pass all stages plus (for many orgs) an explicit approval gate, and results/status are surfaced back to the PR/commit so developers get fast feedback.

stages.prompt: Build queue times balloon during peak hours as hundreds of engineers push code simultaneously, each triggering pipeline runs. How do you scale the build infrastructure?
stages.answer: Run build workers as an autoscaling pool (spinning up more capacity as queue depth grows, scaling down when idle) rather than a fixed-size fleet, and support caching aggressively at every layer (dependency caches, build artifact caches, container layer caches) so most builds don't repeat expensive work from scratch — caching often has a bigger impact on average build time than raw worker count, since most changes are incremental.

stages.prompt: How do you prevent a bad deployment from causing a production incident, given the whole point of CI/CD is fast, frequent deploys?
stages.answer: Combine automated safety with staged rollout: comprehensive automated tests (unit, integration, and ideally some production-like smoke tests) gate the pipeline before deploy, and the deploy itself uses a staged rollout strategy (canary or blue-green) with automated health-check-based rollback — if error rates or latency spike on the new version during the canary phase, the pipeline automatically halts and rolls back rather than continuing to roll out to 100% of traffic, keeping the human out of the loop for the fast, common case while still allowing manual intervention when needed.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Push[Code Push/PR] --> Trigger[Pipeline Trigger]
    Trigger --> Build[Build Stage - cached]
    Build --> Test[Test Stage]
    Test --> Scan[Security Scan]
    Scan -->|approval gate| Deploy[Staged Deploy - canary]
    Deploy -->|health checks pass| FullRollout[Full Rollout]
    Deploy -->|health checks fail| Rollback[Automatic Rollback]
    Workers[Autoscaling Build Workers] -.-> Build

title: Design a Container Registry

stages.prompt: Design a container registry (like Docker Hub or ECR) that lets teams push and pull container images reliably at scale.
stages.answer: Store image layers as content-addressed blobs in object storage (deduplicating identical layers shared across images/tags, which is common since many images share a base layer), with a separate metadata layer tracking repositories, tags, and manifests (which layers make up a given tagged image). Pushing an image uploads any layers not already present (skipping ones the registry already has via content hash) and updates the manifest; pulling fetches the manifest, then any layers the client doesn't already have cached locally.

stages.prompt: A popular base image is pulled thousands of times per minute across a company's build infrastructure, particularly during CI pipeline bursts. How do you keep pull latency low and avoid overloading the registry?
stages.answer: Put a CDN/caching layer in front of the registry's blob storage for image layer downloads, since layers are immutable once pushed (content-addressed) and therefore perfectly cacheable — a popular layer only needs to be fetched from origin once per edge location, with all subsequent pulls served from cache. This is the same fundamental caching strategy as any other high-volume immutable content delivery problem.

stages.prompt: How do you handle image vulnerability scanning and prevent teams from deploying images with known critical vulnerabilities?
stages.answer: Run automated vulnerability scanning on every pushed image (checking installed packages against known-CVE databases) and integrate the scan result into the deployment pipeline as a gate — configurable policies can block deployment of images with critical unpatched vulnerabilities while allowing lower-severity findings through with a warning, and scan results should be visible to teams so they can proactively patch base images rather than only discovering issues at deploy time.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Push[docker push] --> Registry[Registry API]
    Registry -->|dedupe by content hash| BlobStore[(Object Storage - layers)]
    Registry --> Manifests[(Manifest/Tag Metadata)]
    Pull[docker pull] --> CDN[CDN Cache]
    CDN -->|cache miss| BlobStore
    Push --> Scanner[Vulnerability Scanner]
    Scanner -->|blocks critical CVEs| Deploy[Deployment Gate]

title: Design a Serverless Function Platform

stages.prompt: Design the core execution infrastructure for a serverless function platform (like AWS Lambda), where users upload code that runs on-demand without managing servers.
stages.answer: On an invocation request, the platform locates or provisions an execution environment (a lightweight, isolated sandbox — commonly a microVM for strong isolation with fast startup) pre-loaded or quickly loaded with the function's code, runs the function with the provided input, captures the output, and tears down or recycles the environment after execution (or keeps it 'warm' briefly to serve a follow-up request without a fresh cold start). Billing is based on actual execution time and resources consumed, requiring precise per-invocation resource accounting.

stages.prompt: Cold starts (spinning up a fresh execution environment for a function that hasn't run recently) add significant latency, which is bad for latency-sensitive use cases. How do you mitigate this?
stages.answer: Keep a pool of 'warm' pre-initialized environments for frequently-invoked functions rather than tearing down every environment immediately after use, reusing them for subsequent invocations within some idle window before finally recycling. For predictable-traffic use cases, support 'provisioned concurrency' (explicitly keeping N environments warm and ready ahead of expected demand) as an opt-in, paid feature — trading the cost-efficiency of pure on-demand scaling for latency guarantees where that tradeoff matters to the customer.

stages.prompt: How do you ensure strong isolation between different customers' functions running on shared underlying hardware, given the whole platform depends on that isolation being solid?
stages.answer: Use hardware-virtualization-backed isolation (microVMs like Firecracker, rather than just OS-level container namespaces, which offer weaker isolation guarantees) so that even if one function's execution environment were somehow compromised, it couldn't access another customer's data or environment on the same physical host. This isolation guarantee is foundational to the entire platform's trust model, since customers are running arbitrary code on shared infrastructure they don't control.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Invoke[Function Invocation] --> Router[Invocation Router]
    Router -->|warm available| WarmPool[Warm Environment Pool]
    Router -->|cold start needed| Provision[Provision microVM]
    WarmPool --> Execute[Execute Function]
    Provision --> Execute
    Execute -->|output| Caller[Caller]
    Execute -->|recycle or keep warm| WarmPool
    Billing[(Per-invocation Billing)] -.-> Execute

title: Design an Object Storage System

stages.prompt: Design an object storage system (like S3) that durably stores and serves arbitrarily large binary objects at massive scale, with a simple key-based API.
stages.answer: Objects are split and replicated (or erasure-coded, a more storage-efficient alternative to full replication) across multiple physical storage nodes spanning different failure domains (racks, availability zones), with a metadata layer tracking which storage nodes hold which object's data. A PUT writes the object's data to multiple nodes and only acknowledges success once the configured durability requirement (e.g., successfully written to a majority or all replicas) is met; a GET can be served from any node holding a copy.

stages.prompt: How does the system provide the extremely high durability guarantees (like 'eleven nines') that object storage services advertise?
stages.answer: Durability comes from redundancy across independent failure domains (so a single disk, node, rack, or even entire availability zone failure doesn't lose data) combined with continuous background integrity checking (periodically verifying stored data against checksums and automatically re-replicating from a healthy copy if corruption or a lost replica is detected) — durability is a property of ongoing operational vigilance, not just the initial write's redundancy.

stages.prompt: How do you support cost-effective storage for data that's rarely accessed (like old backups or logs) without the customer needing to manage moving it themselves?
stages.answer: Offer storage tiers with different cost/latency/access-frequency tradeoffs (a 'hot' tier for frequently accessed data, cheaper 'cold'/archive tiers with higher retrieval latency or cost for rarely accessed data), and support lifecycle policies that automatically transition objects between tiers based on age or access pattern — this offloads a real cost-optimization problem from every individual customer onto a configurable, automated platform feature.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Client -->|PUT object| API[Object Storage API]
    API -->|replicate/erasure-code| Node1[(Storage Node - AZ1)]
    API --> Node2[(Storage Node - AZ2)]
    API --> Node3[(Storage Node - AZ3)]
    API --> Metadata[(Metadata: key -> node mapping)]
    IntegrityCheck[Background Integrity Checker] -.-> Node1
    IntegrityCheck -.->|re-replicate on failure| Node2
    LifecyclePolicy[Lifecycle Policy] -.->|hot to cold tier| Node1

title: Design a Content Management System

stages.prompt: Design a CMS that lets non-technical content teams create, edit, and publish structured content (articles, pages) that gets rendered on a public website, with draft/review/publish workflow states.
stages.answer: Model content as structured documents with a defined schema (fields like title, body, images, metadata) stored in a database, with each document carrying a status (draft, in review, published) and a version history so edits are non-destructive and reversible. Publishing a document makes it available to the public-facing rendering layer, typically via a cache/CDN invalidation so the change is visible quickly, while unpublished drafts remain accessible only to authorized editors.

stages.prompt: Multiple editors need to collaborate on the same document without overwriting each other's changes, and content needs to go through an approval workflow before publishing. How do you support this?
stages.answer: Support a defined workflow state machine (draft → in review → approved → published, with configurable required approvers) rather than a simple binary published/unpublished flag, and use optimistic concurrency control (each save includes the version it was based on; a conflicting concurrent edit is detected and surfaced to the editor rather than silently overwritten) or real-time collaborative editing (CRDT-based, as in a collaborative document editor) for true simultaneous editing if that's a required use case.

stages.prompt: The public website needs to render content extremely fast globally, but content changes need to appear quickly after publishing. How do you balance caching aggressively with freshness?
stages.answer: Serve published content through a CDN with long cache TTLs for performance, but trigger explicit cache invalidation/purge for the specific affected pages the moment content is published, rather than relying on TTL expiry alone — this gets you both fast global delivery for the common case (unchanged content) and near-immediate freshness for the specific pages that just changed, without needing short TTLs everywhere that would hurt overall cache hit rate.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Editor[Content Editor] -->|draft| CMS[CMS - workflow engine]
    CMS -->|version history| ContentDB[(Content Database)]
    CMS -->|approval workflow| Reviewer[Reviewer/Approver]
    Reviewer -->|approved| Publish[Publish Action]
    Publish -->|cache invalidation| CDN[CDN]
    CDN --> PublicSite[Public Website]

title: Design a Collaborative Whiteboard

stages.prompt: Design a real-time collaborative whiteboard (like Figma or Miro) where multiple users can simultaneously draw, move, and edit shapes on a shared canvas.
stages.answer: Each client holds a local copy of the canvas state and sends granular edit operations (add shape, move shape, change property) over a WebSocket connection to a server, which broadcasts operations to all other connected clients editing the same board; each client applies incoming operations to its local state, keeping all clients' views in sync. Use a CRDT-based data structure for shared state specifically so concurrent edits from different users always converge to the same result regardless of the order operations arrive in, without needing a central lock on any single element.

stages.prompt: Two users drag the same shape simultaneously. How do you handle this so both users see a consistent, sensible result rather than the shape jumping erratically?
stages.answer: With a CRDT-based approach, define the shape's position as a value with a well-defined merge rule for concurrent updates (e.g., last-writer-wins based on a logical clock, or a more sophisticated merge for continuous properties like position) so simultaneous drags converge deterministically rather than one client's update silently overwriting the other's mid-drag in a way that looks broken. Visually, showing other users' live cursor positions and current selections helps users naturally avoid editing the same element simultaneously, reducing how often true conflicts occur in practice.

stages.prompt: How do you support a very large, complex board (thousands of elements) without every client needing to sync the entire board's state on every connection or edit?
