stages.answer: Partition the board into regions/tiles and only sync full detail for the regions currently in a given client's viewport (streaming in more detail as the user pans/zooms), similar to how mapping applications handle large-scale spatial data — a client editing a small corner of a huge board shouldn't need every single element's data pushed to it continuously, only what's relevant to what they can currently see and interact with.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    ClientA[Client A] <-->|WebSocket: ops| Server[Collab Server]
    ClientB[Client B] <-->|WebSocket: ops| Server
    Server -->|CRDT merge| BoardState[(Shared Board State)]
    Server -->|viewport-based sync| ClientA
    Server -->|viewport-based sync| ClientB
    BoardState -->|periodic snapshot| Persist[(Persistent Storage)]

title: Design a Video Conferencing System

stages.prompt: Design the core architecture for a video conferencing system (like Zoom) supporting group calls with many participants.
stages.answer: For group calls beyond a handful of participants, use an SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit) architecture: each participant sends their audio/video stream once to a central media server, which forwards (routes) each participant's stream to every other participant, rather than every participant sending directly to every other participant (which doesn't scale bandwidth-wise, an approach called mesh/P2P that only works for very small calls). Signaling (call setup, who's in the call, ICE/NAT traversal negotiation) is handled by a separate signaling server, decoupled from the actual media path.

stages.prompt: A participant on a poor network connection experiences choppy video that also seems to affect other participants' experience of them. How do you handle variable network quality per participant?
stages.answer: Use simulcast (each sender encodes their video at multiple quality/bitrate levels simultaneously) so the SFU can forward a lower-quality stream to recipients with poor bandwidth without affecting what's sent to recipients with good bandwidth — a struggling participant's own inbound stream to the SFU can also be adaptively downgraded, but this shouldn't force everyone else's view of unrelated participants to degrade too, since the forwarding decision can be made independently per recipient.

stages.prompt: How do you scale to support a call with hundreds or thousands of participants (like a large webinar), where the SFU's forward-everything-to-everyone approach breaks down?
stages.answer: Beyond a certain participant count, shift from a full-mesh SFU model (where every participant potentially receives every other's stream) to a broadcast/webinar model: only a small number of designated presenters' streams are actively forwarded to all viewers, while most participants are receive-only, dramatically reducing the fan-out bandwidth requirement — this is a fundamentally different architecture for a fundamentally different use case (broadcast vs. interactive small-group call), and the system should support switching between them rather than trying to force one model to handle both scales.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    ParticipantA[Participant A] -->|send stream once| SFU[SFU Media Server]
    ParticipantB[Participant B] -->|send stream once| SFU
    SFU -->|forward, simulcast quality per recipient| ParticipantA
    SFU -->|forward| ParticipantB
    SignalingServer[Signaling Server] -.->|call setup, ICE negotiation| ParticipantA
    SignalingServer -.-> ParticipantB
    LargeWebinar[Large Webinar Mode] -.->|broadcast, mostly receive-only| SFU

title: Design a Ticket Booking System

stages.prompt: Design a ticket booking system (like Ticketmaster) for high-demand events, where thousands of users try to book a limited number of seats simultaneously at on-sale time.
stages.answer: Represent seat inventory with strict per-seat state (available, held, sold), and when a user selects seats, place a short-lived hold (e.g., 5-10 minutes) atomically reserving those specific seats for that user while they complete checkout, using an atomic conditional update so two users can never simultaneously hold the same seat. If checkout isn't completed before the hold expires, the seats automatically return to available inventory for others.

stages.prompt: At the exact moment tickets go on sale for a hugely popular event, demand vastly exceeds supply and the system faces an enormous concurrent request spike. How do you handle this without the system falling over or seats being oversold?
stages.answer: Use a virtual waiting room that queues excess demand and admits users to the actual booking flow at a controlled rate the backend can handle, rather than letting the full spike hit the booking system directly — this is the standard pattern for extreme, predictable demand spikes (a known on-sale time), converting an uncontrolled thundering-herd into a controlled, gradual admission rate. For the seat-holding mechanism itself, a fast atomic store (like Redis) handling the hold/release operations avoids the primary database becoming a contention bottleneck at the moment of peak concurrent hold attempts.

stages.prompt: How do you handle payment failures or abandoned checkouts gracefully so held seats don't get stuck unavailable if a user's payment fails or they simply close the tab?
stages.answer: The time-bound hold (from stage 1) is exactly the mechanism that handles this — if checkout doesn't complete (payment fails, or the user abandons) before the hold's TTL expires, the seats are automatically released back to available inventory without requiring any explicit cleanup action, which is important given that relying on catching every possible abandonment scenario explicitly (browser closed, network dropped, etc.) is much less robust than a TTL-based expiry that handles all of them uniformly.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    OnSale[On-sale Traffic Spike] --> WaitingRoom[Virtual Waiting Room]
    WaitingRoom -->|controlled admission rate| BookingFlow[Booking Flow]
    BookingFlow -->|atomic hold, TTL| SeatStore[(Redis Seat Hold Store)]
    BookingFlow -->|checkout| Payment[Payment Processing]
    Payment -->|success| ConfirmedDB[(Confirmed Bookings DB)]
    SeatStore -->|hold expired| SeatStore

title: Design a Food Delivery System

stages.prompt: Design a food delivery platform matching customers, restaurants, and delivery drivers, from order placement through delivery.
stages.answer: Core flow: customer places an order routed to the restaurant (via the platform's order management, integrated with the restaurant's own order-taking system or a tablet), the restaurant confirms and prepares it, and a dispatch system matches an available nearby driver (using a geospatial index of driver locations, similar to a ride-hailing matching system) to pick up and deliver the order — with real-time status updates (preparing, out for delivery, delivered) pushed to the customer throughout.

stages.prompt: How do you estimate and display accurate delivery time estimates to customers, given it depends on restaurant prep time, driver availability, and route time, all of which vary?
stages.answer: Break the estimate into components computed separately: expected prep time (historically modeled per restaurant and possibly per item, since prep time varies a lot by restaurant and order complexity), expected time to match and dispatch a driver (depends on current driver supply/demand in that area), and expected travel time (from a routing/ETA service, accounting for current traffic) — summing these gives a more accurate estimate than a single blanket 'typically takes 30-45 minutes' figure, and each component can be refined independently as more data accumulates.

stages.prompt: During a demand surge (e.g., dinner rush in a popular area), driver supply can't keep up with order volume. How does the system respond?
stages.answer: Similar to ride-hailing surge dynamics: temporarily increase driver incentive pay in high-demand areas to attract more available drivers to reposition there, and communicate realistic (longer) delivery estimates to customers during the surge rather than under-promising — some platforms also temporarily pause new orders from restaurants that are clearly overwhelmed, to prevent a backlog that leads to very late, cold food and a bad experience for everyone in the queue.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Customer[Customer Order] --> OrderMgmt[Order Management]
    OrderMgmt --> Restaurant[Restaurant]
    OrderMgmt --> Dispatch[Driver Dispatch]
    Dispatch --> GeoIndex[(Driver Geospatial Index)]
    Dispatch -->|match| Driver[Delivery Driver]
    ETAService[ETA Service - prep + dispatch + travel] -.-> Customer
    SurgeEngine[Surge Incentive Engine] -.->|high demand area| Driver

title: Design a Hotel Booking System

stages.prompt: Design a hotel booking system that lets users search for available rooms across many hotels by date range and location, and book without double-booking a room.
stages.answer: Model room inventory per hotel per room-type per date (a room-type has N total rooms; each booking decrements available count for its date range), and search queries filter hotels by location/dates against this availability data. Booking a room requires an atomic check-and-decrement across the entire requested date range (all nights must be available) — if any night in the range lacks availability, the whole booking fails, since a partial booking across a date range isn't a valid outcome.

stages.prompt: The system integrates with individual hotels' own property management systems (PMS) for real inventory, which may have latency or occasional inconsistency. How do you prevent double-booking a room the platform thinks is available but the hotel's own system has already sold?
stages.answer: Treat the platform's cached availability as provisional, not authoritative — hold the booking with a short-lived reservation and make a final real-time availability confirmation call to the hotel's PMS before finalizing, so a stale cached view doesn't result in confirming a room that's actually already taken. When a discrepancy is detected, fail gracefully with a clear message and updated availability, rather than confirming an invalid booking that will later need to be canceled after the customer already believes it's confirmed.

stages.prompt: How do you handle cancellation policies and refunds that vary significantly by hotel and rate type (fully refundable vs. non-refundable, free cancellation windows)?
stages.answer: Store the specific cancellation policy as structured data tied to the exact rate/booking at the time of purchase (not just a general hotel-level policy, since the same hotel may offer different rates with different policies), so a cancellation request can be evaluated deterministically against the terms the customer actually agreed to, and refund processing can be automated for clear-cut cases (within the free cancellation window) while flagging edge cases for manual review.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Search[Search: location + dates] --> AvailabilityIndex[(Cached Availability Index)]
    AvailabilityIndex --> Results[Search Results]
    Book[Book Room] -->|provisional hold| ReservationHold[(Reservation Hold)]
    ReservationHold -->|real-time confirm| HotelPMS[Hotel's PMS]
    HotelPMS -->|confirmed| Booking[(Confirmed Booking + Policy)]
    HotelPMS -->|unavailable| Fail[Booking Failed - refresh availability]

title: Design a Stock Trading Platform

stages.prompt: Design the core order-matching engine for a stock trading platform that matches buy and sell orders for a given stock.
stages.answer: Maintain an order book per stock: a sorted structure of buy orders (bids, highest price first) and sell orders (asks, lowest price first). A new order is matched against the opposite side's best-priced orders first (price-time priority: best price first, and among equal prices, earliest order first); a match executes a trade at the matched price, and any unmatched remainder of the order rests in the book waiting for a future match. This matching logic needs to be extremely fast and deterministic, since correctness (never losing or duplicating an order) and fairness (strict price-time priority) are both non-negotiable requirements.

stages.prompt: The matching engine must process orders with extremely low, consistent latency (microseconds matter to some traders) and must never lose an order even during a crash. How do you design for this?
stages.answer: Run the matching engine as a highly optimized, often single-threaded-per-symbol in-memory process (avoiding the overhead and unpredictability of distributed coordination on the hot matching path) with orders processed strictly sequentially per symbol to preserve deterministic price-time priority, while durably logging every order and match event (write-ahead logging) before acknowledging it, so a crash can replay the log to reconstruct exact state rather than losing or reordering trades — durability and extreme low-latency are both required simultaneously, which is why this differs architecturally from a typical high-throughput web service.

stages.prompt: How do you ensure regulatory compliance and auditability, given every trade must be fully explainable and reportable?
stages.answer: Persist an immutable, complete audit trail of every order (submitted, modified, canceled, matched) with precise timestamps, sufficient to reconstruct exactly why any given trade executed at the price and time it did — this audit log is a hard regulatory requirement in most jurisdictions, not an optional nice-to-have, and needs to be designed in from the start (as a natural byproduct of the write-ahead logging used for durability) rather than bolted on afterward.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    BuyOrder[Buy Order] --> MatchingEngine[Matching Engine - per symbol]
    SellOrder[Sell Order] --> MatchingEngine
    MatchingEngine --> OrderBook[(In-memory Order Book\nprice-time priority)]
    MatchingEngine -->|write-ahead log| DurableLog[(Durable Order/Trade Log)]
    MatchingEngine -->|match| TradeExecution[Trade Execution]
    DurableLog --> AuditTrail[(Regulatory Audit Trail)]

title: Design a Cryptocurrency Exchange

stages.prompt: Design a cryptocurrency exchange that lets users deposit crypto, trade between currency pairs, and withdraw funds.
stages.answer: Similar order-matching-engine core as a stock exchange (order book, price-time priority matching) for the trading component, plus a separate wallet/custody system tracking each user's balance per currency (most of which is held in the exchange's own pooled wallets, not literally on-chain per user, for operational efficiency) and processing deposits (crediting a user's balance once an on-chain transaction reaches sufficient confirmations) and withdrawals (debiting balance and initiating an on-chain transaction).

stages.prompt: Custody of user funds is the single highest-stakes part of the system — a compromise here means stolen customer funds. How do you architect wallet security?
stages.answer: Use a hot/cold wallet split: keep only a small operational fraction of total funds in 'hot' wallets (connected to the internet, needed for processing real-time withdrawals) and the vast majority in 'cold' storage (offline, air-gapped, requiring manual/multi-party authorization to move), so even a full compromise of the hot wallet's systems limits losses to a bounded, small fraction of total customer funds rather than everything. Require multi-signature authorization (multiple independent parties/keys) for any cold-to-hot wallet transfer, so no single compromised credential or insider can unilaterally move large sums.

stages.prompt: How do you handle the fact that on-chain transactions (deposits/withdrawals) are slower and less immediately final than the exchange's own internal ledger updates?
stages.answer: Require a currency-specific number of block confirmations before crediting a deposit to a user's tradeable balance (balancing the risk of a blockchain reorg reversing an unconfirmed transaction against not wanting to make users wait unnecessarily long), and process withdrawals as an internal balance debit immediately (for the user's view) while the actual on-chain transaction is queued and broadcast — clearly communicating that the withdrawal is 'processing' until the on-chain transaction actually confirms, since the internal ledger update and the real on-chain settlement are two distinct events with different timing.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    User[User] -->|deposit| OnChainMonitor[On-chain Deposit Monitor]
    OnChainMonitor -->|N confirmations| LedgerService[Internal Ledger Service]
    User -->|trade| MatchingEngine[Order Matching Engine]
    MatchingEngine --> LedgerService
    LedgerService --> HotWallet[(Hot Wallet - small %)]
    LedgerService --> ColdWallet[(Cold Wallet - majority, multi-sig)]
    User -->|withdraw| WithdrawalQueue[Withdrawal Queue]
    WithdrawalQueue --> HotWallet

title: Design a Digital Wallet

stages.prompt: Design a digital wallet system (like a mobile payment app) that lets users store a balance, send/receive money to other users, and link external funding sources (bank accounts, cards).
stages.answer: Maintain each user's balance as a ledger (following the double-entry bookkeeping principles common to financial systems: every transfer is a debit from one account and a credit to another within a single atomic transaction), support topping up the wallet balance from a linked external funding source (via a payment processor integration) and withdrawing back out, and support instant peer-to-peer transfers between two wallet users as a pure internal ledger operation (fast, since it doesn't need to touch any external payment rail).

stages.prompt: A user tries to send money they don't actually have (race condition: two simultaneous transfers both check 'sufficient balance' before either completes). How do you prevent overdrafts?
stages.answer: Perform the balance check and the debit as a single atomic operation (a conditional update — decrement balance only if it stays non-negative — executed within a database transaction, not a separate read-then-write from application code, which is vulnerable to exactly this race condition), so two concurrent transfer attempts against the same balance can't both succeed if their combined total exceeds available funds, regardless of timing.

stages.prompt: How do you handle a transfer to an external bank account, which — unlike the instant internal peer-to-peer case — takes real time (often 1-3 business days) to actually settle?
stages.answer: Reflect the transfer as an immediate internal ledger debit and a 'pending' external transfer, keeping those two concepts distinct (the user's wallet balance drops immediately as the funds are committed to leaving, but the actual bank transfer is an asynchronous process tracked separately with its own status) — clearly communicate the pending state to the user, and handle the failure case (a bank transfer that ultimately fails or is rejected) by reversing the internal ledger entry, since the two systems (internal ledger, external bank rail) don't update atomically together and need explicit reconciliation logic for failure scenarios.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    User[User] -->|top up| ExternalFunding[Linked Bank/Card]
    ExternalFunding --> Ledger[(Internal Wallet Ledger\ndouble-entry)]
    User -->|P2P transfer| Ledger
    Ledger -->|atomic conditional debit| Ledger
    User -->|withdraw| PendingTransfer[Pending External Transfer]
    PendingTransfer --> BankRail[Bank Transfer Rail - 1-3 days]
    BankRail -->|failure| Reversal[Reverse Ledger Entry]

title: Design a Subscription Billing System

stages.prompt: Design a subscription billing system that handles recurring charges for a SaaS product, including plan changes, proration, and failed payment retries.
stages.answer: Model each customer's subscription with a defined billing cycle (e.g., monthly), and run a scheduled billing job that, for each subscription due, generates an invoice and attempts to charge the customer's stored payment method via a payment processor, recording the outcome. Plan upgrades/downgrades mid-cycle require proration logic (crediting/charging the difference for the remaining portion of the current billing period) computed based on the exact time remaining in the cycle.

stages.prompt: A recurring charge fails (expired card, insufficient funds). How do you handle this without immediately cutting off the customer's access or losing the revenue unnecessarily?
stages.answer: Implement a dunning process: retry the failed charge on a defined schedule (e.g., a few attempts over 1-2 weeks, since many failures are transient — a card that's temporarily over its limit, for instance) while sending the customer notifications to update their payment method, only suspending or canceling access after retries are exhausted without success — abrupt immediate cutoff on the first failed attempt loses revenue from what are often easily recoverable, temporary payment issues.

stages.prompt: How do you ensure billing calculations (especially proration across plan changes) are always auditable and correct, given billing mistakes directly cost the company money or damage customer trust?
stages.answer: Generate an explicit, itemized invoice for every billing event (showing exactly what was charged and why — base plan charge, proration credit/charge, any add-ons) rather than just debiting a lump sum, and treat invoices as immutable once issued (corrections happen via a new adjusting invoice/credit note, not by editing history) so there's always a clear, auditable record explaining any charge a customer or support team might question later.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Scheduler[Billing Scheduler] -->|cycle due| InvoiceGen[Invoice Generation\nwith proration]
    InvoiceGen --> Charge[Charge Attempt]
    Charge -->|payment processor| PaymentProcessor[Payment Processor]
    Charge -->|success| Paid[(Paid Invoice)]
    Charge -->|failure| Dunning[Dunning: retry schedule + notify]
    Dunning -->|exhausted| Suspend[Suspend Access]
    Paid --> AuditTrail[(Invoice Audit Trail)]

title: Design a Real-Time Bidding Ad Exchange

stages.prompt: Design a real-time bidding (RTB) ad exchange that, when a user loads a page with an ad slot, solicits bids from multiple advertisers and selects a winner, all within roughly 100ms.
stages.answer: On an ad request, the exchange broadcasts a bid request (containing anonymized user/context signals) to multiple demand-side platforms (DSPs) simultaneously, each of which must return a bid within a strict timeout (commonly under 100ms total for the whole auction); the exchange runs an auction (commonly second-price: highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid) among the responses received in time, and the winning ad is returned to render in the slot — any DSP that doesn't respond within the timeout is simply excluded from that auction.

stages.prompt: With dozens of DSPs and a hard ~100ms budget, how do you keep the whole system fast even though you're waiting on multiple external network calls?
stages.answer: Fan out bid requests to all DSPs in parallel (never sequentially) with a strict per-DSP timeout, and proceed to auction resolution using whichever bids arrived in time rather than waiting for stragglers — a DSP that's occasionally slow just loses out on that specific auction rather than holding up the entire request. Geographic proximity between the exchange and DSP endpoints (or requiring DSPs to have low-latency endpoints as an integration requirement) also directly determines how many DSPs can realistically participate within the tight budget.

stages.prompt: How do you prevent fraud (fake bid requests, bots inflating impression counts) from undermining trust in the exchange for both advertisers and publishers?
stages.answer: Apply bot/fraud detection at multiple points: filtering known bot traffic patterns and non-human signals before even generating a bid request, requiring publishers to be vetted/verified (reducing fake-inventory fraud from malicious publishers), and providing advertisers with post-auction verification/reporting so discrepancies (impressions billed but not verifiably delivered to real users) can be caught, refunded, and used to identify and remove bad actors from the exchange over time.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    PageLoad[Page Load - Ad Slot] --> Exchange[Ad Exchange]
    Exchange -->|parallel bid request, ~100ms timeout| DSP1[DSP 1]
    Exchange -->|parallel| DSP2[DSP 2]
    Exchange -->|parallel| DSP3[DSP 3]
    DSP1 --> Auction[Second-Price Auction]
    DSP2 --> Auction
    Auction -->|winner| AdRender[Ad Rendered]
    FraudDetection[Fraud Detection] -.-> Exchange

title: Design a Full-Text Search Engine

stages.prompt: Design a full-text search engine (like a simplified Elasticsearch) that indexes documents and supports fast keyword search with relevance ranking.
stages.answer: Build an inverted index: for each unique term across all documents, store a list of which documents contain it (and typically term frequency/position information for ranking and phrase queries). A search query is tokenized into terms, the index is looked up for each term to find candidate documents, and results are ranked by a relevance scoring function (commonly TF-IDF or BM25, which weigh how important a term is to a document relative to the whole corpus) rather than just returning unranked matches.

stages.prompt: The document corpus is too large for a single machine's inverted index. How do you shard the index and still return accurate, well-ranked results?
stages.answer: Shard the inverted index across multiple nodes (commonly by document, so each shard holds a complete index for its subset of documents), and for each query, fan out to all shards, have each shard return its locally top-ranked results, then merge and re-rank at a coordinating layer — this is the same scatter-gather pattern used for distributed vector search, and it requires care with global term statistics (like document frequency, used in TF-IDF/BM25 scoring) since a purely per-shard-local calculation can produce ranking that's slightly inconsistent with what a single global index would produce, though this is often an acceptable approximation in practice.

stages.prompt: How do you keep the index up to date as documents are added, updated, and deleted continuously, without full reindexing becoming a bottleneck?
stages.answer: Support incremental indexing (new/changed documents are indexed and merged into the existing index structure without rebuilding everything), commonly using a segment-based approach where new documents go into small new index segments that are periodically merged with older segments in the background — this is the standard technique (used by Lucene/Elasticsearch) for supporting continuous writes without either blocking search availability or requiring disruptive full rebuilds.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Document[New/Updated Document] --> Indexer[Indexer]
    Indexer -->|new segment| Shard1[(Shard 1 - Inverted Index)]
    Indexer -->|new segment| Shard2[(Shard 2)]
    BackgroundMerge[Background Segment Merge] -.-> Shard1
    Query[Search Query] --> Coordinator[Query Coordinator]
    Coordinator -->|scatter| Shard1
    Coordinator -->|scatter| Shard2
    Shard1 -->|local top-k, ranked| Coordinator
    Coordinator -->|merge + re-rank| Results[Ranked Results]

title: Design a Data Warehouse / ETL Pipeline

stages.prompt: Design a data pipeline that extracts data from many operational source systems (databases, event streams, third-party APIs), transforms it, and loads it into a data warehouse for analytics.
stages.answer: Extract data from sources (via database change-data-capture for operational DBs, consuming from event streams for real-time data, and scheduled API pulls for third-party sources), land it in raw form in cheap storage first (a 'data lake' staging area), then run transformation jobs that clean, join, and reshape the raw data into well-structured tables optimized for analytical queries in the warehouse — separating extraction/landing from transformation makes each stage independently debuggable and lets you reprocess historical raw data if a transformation bug is found later.

stages.prompt: A transformation job has a bug that produced incorrect data for the last week, and this has already propagated into downstream dashboards and reports that business stakeholders have been using. How do you handle this?
stages.answer: Because raw source data was preserved in the staging/lake layer (not discarded after the first transformation), you can fix the transformation logic and reprocess the affected date range from the preserved raw data to regenerate correct warehouse tables, rather than the bug being unrecoverable. Communicate clearly to downstream consumers about what data was affected and when the correction will be complete, and consider adding automated data-quality checks (row counts, key business metric sanity checks) that would have caught this class of error before it reached dashboards.

stages.prompt: How do you handle schema evolution — a source system adds a new field, or changes a field's type — without breaking the pipeline or losing historical data consistency?
stages.answer: Design the pipeline to handle schema evolution gracefully (e.g., new fields are additive and don't break existing transformations reading older records, and breaking changes like a field type change are handled via explicit versioning of the schema/transformation logic) rather than assuming the source schema is fixed forever. Validate incoming data against an expected schema at ingestion and alert on unexpected changes, so schema drift is caught and handled deliberately rather than silently corrupting downstream data or causing an opaque pipeline failure.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    SourceDB[(Operational DB - CDC)] --> Lake[(Raw Data Lake - staging)]
    EventStream[Event Stream] --> Lake
    ThirdPartyAPI[Third-party API] --> Lake
    Lake --> Transform[Transformation Jobs]
    Transform --> Warehouse[(Data Warehouse)]
    Warehouse --> Dashboards[BI Dashboards]
    QualityChecks[Data Quality Checks] -.-> Transform
    Lake -.->|reprocess on bug fix| Transform

title: Design a Real-Time Analytics Dashboard

stages.prompt: Design a dashboard that shows near-real-time metrics (like current active users, orders per minute) for a high-traffic application, updating within seconds of events happening.
stages.answer: Stream events into a stream-processing job (Kafka Streams, Flink, or similar) that maintains windowed aggregates (e.g., a rolling count of orders in the last minute) incrementally as events arrive, writing current aggregate values to a fast-read store (like Redis) that the dashboard queries or subscribes to — this avoids querying and aggregating raw event data on every dashboard refresh, which wouldn't scale to real-time update frequency at high event volume.

stages.prompt: The dashboard needs to support drilling down into different dimensions (metrics by region, by product category) without precomputing every possible combination in advance.
stages.answer: Precompute aggregates along the most commonly-needed dimension combinations (based on actual usage patterns) rather than every theoretically possible combination, which grows combinatorially and is usually wasteful — for less common ad-hoc drill-down needs, fall back to querying a more detailed (but still reasonably fast) store like a columnar analytical database that isn't pre-aggregated but is optimized for scanning and grouping large amounts of raw event data quickly, accepting slightly higher latency for these less-common queries.

stages.prompt: How do you handle the dashboard staying accurate/consistent if the underlying stream processing job restarts or briefly falls behind?
stages.answer: Design the streaming aggregation to be resumable from a checkpoint (so a restart continues from where it left off rather than resetting or reprocessing everything) and make the dashboard clearly indicate data freshness/lag (e.g., 'as of 12 seconds ago') so users understand they're looking at near-real-time, not necessarily perfectly-current data — being transparent about lag is better than presenting stale data as if it were fully current.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Events[Application Events] --> StreamProcessor[Stream Processor\nwindowed aggregation]
    StreamProcessor -->|checkpointed| FastStore[(Redis - current aggregates)]
    FastStore --> Dashboard[Real-time Dashboard]
    Events --> ColumnarDB[(Columnar Analytical DB - raw events)]
    Dashboard -->|ad-hoc drill-down| ColumnarDB
    StreamProcessor -.->|freshness indicator| Dashboard

title: Design a Multiplayer Game Leaderboard

stages.prompt: Design a leaderboard system for a game with millions of active players, supporting real-time score updates and fast 'get top N' and 'get a specific player's rank' queries.
stages.answer: Use a sorted-set data structure (like Redis's ZSET) keyed by score, which natively supports O(log n) score updates and O(log n + k) range queries (top N, or a player's rank via a rank-lookup operation) — purpose-built for exactly this leaderboard access pattern, far more efficient than running a SQL ORDER BY query against a regular table for every leaderboard request at this scale and update frequency.

stages.prompt: The game has hundreds of millions of players globally. A single sorted set on one Redis instance won't hold this, and global rank queries need to stay fast. How do you scale this?
stages.answer: Shard the leaderboard (e.g., by region, or by a hash of player ID if a single global ranking is needed) across multiple Redis instances, and for a true global top-N query, merge the top candidates from each shard at a coordinating layer — similar to distributed search/vector-index scatter-gather patterns. For 'get a specific player's global rank' at massive scale, an exact real-time global rank across hundreds of millions of sharded entries can be genuinely expensive; consider whether an approximate rank (updated periodically) is an acceptable tradeoff for that specific query, even if top-N and per-shard rank stay exact and real-time.

stages.prompt: How do you support both an all-time leaderboard and a weekly/seasonal leaderboard that resets, without maintaining completely separate score-tracking logic?
stages.answer: Maintain separate sorted sets per time window (all-time, current week, current season), updating all relevant ones on every score event rather than trying to derive time-windowed rankings from a single all-time structure after the fact — this trades a bit of extra write work (updating multiple sorted sets per score event) for very fast, purpose-built reads on each leaderboard variant, which is the right tradeoff given leaderboards are read far more often than scores are updated.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    ScoreEvent[Player Score Event] --> Update[Update Sorted Sets]
    Update --> AllTimeLB[(All-time Leaderboard - sharded ZSET)]
    Update --> WeeklyLB[(Weekly Leaderboard)]
    Query[Top N / Player Rank] --> Coordinator[Query Coordinator]
    Coordinator -->|scatter| AllTimeLB
    Coordinator -->|merge| Result[Leaderboard Result]

title: Design a Social Graph (Friend/Follow) System

stages.prompt: Design a system that stores and queries a social graph (who follows whom) for a platform with hundreds of millions of users, supporting queries like 'who does this user follow' and 'who follows this user' efficiently.
stages.answer: Store the graph as an adjacency-list structure, typically two indexes (a 'following' list per user and a 'followers' list per user, maintained together on every follow/unfollow event) in a database optimized for this access pattern (a wide-column store or a graph database, depending on query complexity needed) — since both directions are queried frequently, denormalizing into both indexes trades some write amplification for much faster reads of either direction, which is the right tradeoff given follow relationships are read far more often than they change.

stages.prompt: A small number of users (celebrities) have tens of millions of followers, creating extreme skew — most users have a normal-sized follower list, a few have an enormous one. How does this affect your design?
stages.answer: This is the same skew problem that shows up in feed fan-out design: operations that need to touch every follower of a celebrity account (like fanning out a new post to followers' feeds) become disproportionately expensive for these accounts specifically, so such operations often need special-cased handling for high-follower-count accounts (e.g., pull-based feed merging instead of push-based fan-out, as discussed in feed system design) rather than assuming uniform behavior works for every account regardless of follower count.

stages.prompt: How do you efficiently answer 'mutual friends/followers' or 'people you may know' style queries, which require intersecting large sets?
stages.answer: For mutual-connections queries, intersecting two users' follow lists directly can be done efficiently if both lists are stored in a structure supporting fast set intersection (sorted lists allow an efficient merge-based intersection); for 'people you may know' style recommendations at scale, this typically shifts from a live graph query to a precomputed, periodically-refreshed batch job (analyzing the graph offline to generate suggestions, since computing 'friends of friends with the most mutual connections' live for every user on every page load doesn't scale, but a daily/hourly batch recomputation feeding a fast lookup table does).

diagram:
flowchart LR
    FollowEvent[Follow/Unfollow Event] --> UpdateBoth[Update Both Indexes]
    UpdateBoth --> FollowingIdx[(Following Index - per user)]
    UpdateBoth --> FollowersIdx[(Followers Index - per user)]
    Query[Who does X follow?] --> FollowingIdx
    Query2[Who follows X?] --> FollowersIdx
    BatchJob[Batch Recommendation Job] -.->|offline graph analysis| SuggestionsTable[(People You May Know Table)]
    CelebrityAccount[Celebrity Account] -.->|special-cased fan-out| UpdateBoth

title: Design a Notification Preference Center

stages.prompt: Design a system that lets users configure granular notification preferences (which types of notifications, via which channels — email/push/SMS — and how often) that every part of the platform must respect before sending any notification.
stages.answer: Store user preferences as structured rules (per notification category, per channel, opted in/out, plus settings like quiet hours or digest frequency) in a central preference service, and require every notification-sending code path across the platform to check this service before actually dispatching — centralizing this rather than letting each feature team implement their own opt-out logic, which reliably leads to inconsistent behavior and users receiving notifications they explicitly turned off.

stages.prompt: How do you ensure a new feature team adding a new notification type doesn't accidentally bypass the preference system (a common way products end up over-notifying users)?
stages.answer: Make respecting preferences structurally difficult to skip rather than a convention to remember — route all notification sending through a shared notification service/library that enforces the preference check internally, so a team can't trivially call an email API directly and bypass the check; require every new notification type to be registered with a default preference and category as part of onboarding it into the shared system, making the 'right' path also the easy, natural path.

stages.prompt: A user wants to see a clear, understandable settings page rather than an overwhelming grid of every possible notification type × channel combination. How do you balance granular control against usability?
stages.answer: Group related notification types into sensible categories with reasonable defaults (most users won't want to configure every single individual setting), expose the most commonly-adjusted controls prominently (like a global 'pause all notifications' or per-channel toggles), and offer granular per-type control as a secondary, discoverable but not default-visible option — the preference *system* underneath can be fully granular even if the *UI* defaults to a simpler, more digestible view for most users.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    FeatureTeam[Feature Team - new notification] --> NotificationLib[Shared Notification Service]
    NotificationLib -->|check first| PreferenceService[(Preference Service)]
    PreferenceService -->|allowed| Dispatch[Dispatch: email/push/SMS]
    PreferenceService -->|opted out| Skip[Skipped]
    User[User Settings Page] --> PreferenceService

title: Design an Email Delivery System

stages.prompt: Design an email delivery system (like SendGrid) that reliably sends transactional and bulk emails on behalf of customers, at high volume.
stages.answer: Accept email send requests via an API, queue them for asynchronous processing (decoupling the customer's request from actual delivery, which can take time and retries), and have worker processes pull from the queue to actually connect to recipient mail servers via SMTP and deliver — tracking delivery status (sent, bounced, deferred) per message and exposing this back to the customer via webhooks or a status API.

stages.prompt: Email deliverability (avoiding spam folders) depends heavily on sender reputation. How do you protect the platform's overall sending reputation given many different customers are sending through shared infrastructure?
stages.answer: Use dedicated or reputation-isolated IP pools segmented by sender trust level/volume (so one customer sending spammy or poorly-targeted email doesn't damage deliverability for other customers sharing the same sending IPs), enforce authentication standards (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) on all outgoing mail, and actively monitor bounce/complaint rates per customer, automatically throttling or suspending senders whose metrics indicate they're likely to trigger spam filters or damage the platform's reputation with mailbox providers.

stages.prompt: How do you handle a large customer sending a bulk campaign to millions of recipients without overwhelming the system or getting the whole batch blocked by a receiving mail provider's rate limits?
stages.answer: Rate-limit outbound sending per destination mail provider (since providers like Gmail/Outlook enforce their own receiving rate limits and will start rejecting or throttling a sender that exceeds them), spreading a large batch's delivery over an appropriate time window rather than attempting to blast it all simultaneously, and prioritize or stagger sending intelligently (e.g., warming up sending volume gradually for a new large campaign) to stay within what receiving providers will accept without triggering spam-like sending pattern detection.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Customer[Customer API Request] --> Queue[(Send Queue)]
    Queue --> Worker[Delivery Worker]
    Worker -->|rate-limited per provider| MailProvider[Recipient Mail Provider]
    Worker --> StatusTracking[(Delivery Status Tracking)]
    StatusTracking -->|webhook| Customer
    ReputationMonitor[Reputation Monitor] -.->|throttle bad senders| Worker
    IPPools[Segmented IP Pools] -.-> Worker

title: Design a Website Uptime Monitoring System

stages.prompt: Design a system (like Pingdom) that monitors thousands of customers' websites/APIs from multiple geographic locations, alerting customers when their site goes down.
stages.answer: Run monitoring checks (HTTP requests to configured URLs, checking status code/response time/content) on a schedule from a distributed fleet of checker nodes in multiple geographic regions, since checking from only one location can't distinguish 'the site is actually down' from 'there's a network issue specific to that one location.' Only declare a site down (and alert) once a majority or configurable threshold of checker locations agree it's unreachable, avoiding false alarms from a single location's transient network blip.

stages.prompt: How do you avoid alerting on transient blips (a site that's briefly slow or has one failed check but recovers immediately) while still alerting quickly on a genuine outage?
stages.answer: Require a small number of consecutive failures (e.g., 2-3 failed checks in a row, not just one) before declaring an outage and alerting, trading a little detection latency for a big reduction in false-positive alerts — the exact threshold is a tunable tradeoff customers can often configure themselves based on how sensitive they want alerting to be for their specific service's tolerance for brief blips versus needing fast detection.

stages.prompt: How do you scale the monitoring checker fleet to handle checking hundreds of thousands of URLs at various check frequencies (some every minute, some every 5 minutes) without checks falling behind schedule?
stages.answer: Use a distributed scheduling system where checks are queued with their due time, and a pool of checker workers (per region) pull due checks and execute them, autoscaling worker capacity based on the total check volume and desired check frequencies — treat 'a check ran late' as a monitored operational metric itself (since a monitoring system that silently falls behind on its own checks defeats the purpose), alerting the platform operators if checks are systematically running behind schedule.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Scheduler[Check Scheduler] --> RegionA[Checker Fleet - Region A]
    Scheduler --> RegionB[Checker Fleet - Region B]
    Scheduler --> RegionC[Checker Fleet - Region C]
    RegionA -->|check result| Aggregator[Result Aggregator]
    RegionB --> Aggregator
    RegionC --> Aggregator
    Aggregator -->|majority agree down, N consecutive failures| AlertEngine[Alert Engine]
    AlertEngine --> Customer[Customer Notification]

title: Design a Distributed Task Queue

stages.prompt: Design a distributed task queue system (like Celery) that lets application code enqueue background jobs (send an email, process an image) to be executed asynchronously by a pool of worker processes.
stages.answer: Producers push serialized task descriptions (function reference plus arguments) onto a durable message broker (like RabbitMQ or Redis); a pool of worker processes consume tasks from the queue, execute them, and report success/failure — decoupling the requesting code (which just needs to enqueue and move on) from the actual execution timing and capacity, which can scale independently by adding more workers.

stages.prompt: A worker crashes while processing a task (e.g., the machine dies mid-execution). How do you ensure the task isn't silently lost?
stages.answer: Use acknowledgment-based delivery: a worker only removes a task from the queue after successfully completing it and explicitly acknowledging (not immediately upon receiving it) — if a worker dies before acknowledging, the broker redelivers the task to another worker after a visibility timeout, ensuring at-least-once execution. This means task handlers should be designed to be idempotent (safe to run more than once) since a crash right after completing work but before the acknowledgment is received would cause a legitimate redelivery of already-completed work.

stages.prompt: Some tasks are quick (send a notification) and some are slow (process a large video file). How do you prevent slow tasks from starving quick ones behind them in the same queue?
stages.answer: Use separate queues per task type/priority (or at least separate 'fast' and 'slow' queues) with dedicated worker pools sized appropriately for each, rather than a single shared queue and worker pool where a burst of slow tasks can back up quick, latency-sensitive tasks behind them — this is directly analogous to the queueing/prioritization problem in any task-scheduling system, and the fix is the same: don't force fundamentally different workloads to share the same queue and resource pool if their latency requirements differ significantly.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Producer[Application] -->|enqueue| FastQueue[(Fast Task Queue)]
    Producer -->|enqueue| SlowQueue[(Slow Task Queue)]
    FastQueue --> FastWorkers[Fast Worker Pool]
    SlowQueue --> SlowWorkers[Slow Worker Pool]
    FastWorkers -->|ack on completion| FastQueue
    FastWorkers -.->|crash before ack| Redelivery[Redelivered after timeout]

title: Design a Blue-Green / Canary Deployment System

stages.prompt: Design a deployment system that lets teams roll out new application versions with minimal risk, supporting both blue-green and canary deployment strategies.
stages.answer: Blue-green: maintain two identical production environments (blue = current live, green = new version), deploy and fully validate the new version in green while blue keeps serving all traffic, then switch traffic to green atomically (via load balancer/DNS cutover) once validated — giving an instant rollback (switch back to blue) if anything's wrong. Canary: instead of an all-at-once switch, gradually shift a small then increasing percentage of traffic to the new version while monitoring health metrics, only proceeding to full rollout if metrics stay healthy at each step.

stages.prompt: For the canary strategy, how do you decide automatically whether to proceed to the next traffic percentage or roll back, without requiring a human to babysit every deployment?
stages.answer: Define explicit health metrics and thresholds up front (error rate, latency percentiles, any business-critical metric) that the deployment system checks automatically at each canary stage, only progressing to the next traffic percentage if metrics stay within acceptable bounds for a defined observation window, and automatically rolling back if they breach the threshold — this automated gate is what makes frequent, low-risk deployment actually practical at scale, since requiring a human to manually watch every single deployment doesn't scale to a team shipping many times a day.

stages.prompt: Blue-green deployment requires running two full production environments simultaneously during a deploy, which is expensive for large services. How do you address this cost, or is canary strictly better?
stages.answer: This is a genuine tradeoff to state explicitly: blue-green gives instant, clean rollback and full pre-switch validation at the cost of doubled infrastructure during the deploy window, while canary uses infrastructure more efficiently (gradually shifting existing capacity rather than doubling it) but has more complex rollback (some users already got the new version) and a longer exposure window before full validation. Many organizations use canary as the default for routine deploys and reserve blue-green for especially risky changes (like a major version upgrade or database migration) where the extra cost of full pre-switch validation and instant rollback is worth paying for.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    NewVersion[New Version] --> Canary[Canary: 5% traffic]
    Canary -->|health checks pass| Canary25[25% traffic]
    Canary25 -->|health checks pass| Canary100[100% traffic]
    Canary -->|health checks fail| Rollback[Automatic Rollback]
    BlueGreen[Blue-Green Alt] --> Green[Green Env - full validation]
    Green -->|validated| Switch[Atomic Traffic Switch]
    Switch -.->|instant rollback available| Blue[Blue Env - kept warm]

title: Design a Photo/Video Sharing App

stages.prompt: Design the core architecture for a photo/video sharing app (like Instagram) supporting uploads, a personalized feed, and stories that expire after 24 hours.
stages.answer: Upload flow: media is uploaded to object storage, triggering an async processing pipeline (resizing/transcoding into multiple resolutions, generating thumbnails), with metadata (caption, owner, timestamp) stored in a database. Feed generation uses the hybrid push/pull fan-out pattern discussed in news feed design (push to followers' feed lists for normal accounts, pull-and-merge at read time for high-follower accounts), and stories use a similar storage/delivery path but with a TTL-based expiration (either a scheduled cleanup job or simply filtering expired stories out at read time, with actual deletion happening later via a lower-priority cleanup process).

stages.prompt: How do you efficiently serve images/videos at the right resolution for each user's specific device and network conditions, given the same photo needs to look good on everything from a small phone to a large tablet?
stages.answer: Generate and store multiple resolution variants of each uploaded image/video at upload time (not on-demand per request, which would add latency), and have the client request the appropriate variant based on its screen size and current network conditions (adaptively choosing lower resolution on a poor connection, similar to adaptive bitrate video streaming), served through a CDN for low-latency global delivery of whichever variant is requested.

stages.prompt: How do you handle the write-heavy, bursty nature of 'stories' (many users posting frequently, all expiring on a rolling 24-hour basis) differently from permanent feed posts?
stages.answer: Stories can use a simpler storage/retrieval model than the permanent feed specifically because of their short lifespan and typically smaller total viewership per story compared to a viral permanent post — a lighter-weight, TTL-native store (rather than the more complex, permanently-indexed feed infrastructure) is often sufficient, and the natural expiration means storage costs and index size stay bounded automatically without needing the same long-term archival/cold-storage tiering strategy the permanent feed's media needs.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Upload[Media Upload] --> ObjectStore[(Object Storage)]
    Upload --> ProcessingPipeline[Async Transcode/Resize Pipeline]
    ProcessingPipeline --> Variants[(Multiple Resolution Variants)]
    Variants --> CDN[CDN]
    Upload -->|normal account| FanOut[Push to Follower Feeds]
    Upload -->|celebrity account| PullMerge[Pull-merge at Read Time]
    StoryUpload[Story Upload] --> TTLStore[(TTL-based Story Store)]
    TTLStore -->|24h expiry| Expired[Expired/Cleaned Up]

title: Design a Music Streaming Service

stages.prompt: Design a music streaming service (like Spotify) supporting on-demand playback of a huge catalog, playlists, and offline downloads.
stages.answer: Store audio files (encoded at multiple bitrates) in object storage, served through a CDN for playback (streaming, not fully downloading, unless offline mode is used); a metadata service tracks the catalog (tracks, albums, artists), user library/playlists, and playback history. Offline downloads store the audio file (encrypted, DRM-protected) locally on the device with playback rights tied to an active subscription, requiring periodic online license/subscription-validity checks even while primarily playing offline.

stages.prompt: How does the system generate personalized recommendations (like a 'Discover Weekly' style playlist) at the scale of hundreds of millions of users and tens of millions of tracks?
stages.answer: This follows the standard large-scale recommendation architecture: offline batch jobs compute user and track embeddings (via collaborative filtering on listening behavior, and content-based signals from audio/metadata analysis) periodically, feeding a candidate-generation step (fast approximate retrieval of plausible tracks for a user) followed by a ranking step that scores and orders the smaller candidate set — generating a full personalized playlist doesn't need to happen in real time on every request, since these are typically precomputed on a schedule (e.g., weekly) rather than needing to reflect the last few seconds of listening.

stages.prompt: How do you handle royalty/rights tracking, given every single play needs to be counted accurately for artist payouts, at massive play volume?
stages.answer: Log every playback event (track, user, timestamp, duration listened — since royalty rules often require a minimum listen duration to count as a 'play') to a durable, high-throughput event pipeline, and run batch aggregation jobs (periodically, e.g., daily) to compute accurate per-track, per-territory play counts feeding into royalty calculations — this needs to be exactly correct and auditable given it directly determines real payments to rights holders, so the pipeline design prioritizes completeness and auditability of the event log over pure real-time speed for this specific use case.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    AudioFile[Audio Catalog] --> ObjectStore[(Object Storage - multi-bitrate)]
    ObjectStore --> CDN[CDN]
    User[User] -->|stream| CDN
    User -->|offline download| LocalStorage[Encrypted Local Storage]
    PlaybackEvent[Playback Events] --> RoyaltyPipeline[(Royalty Event Pipeline)]
    RoyaltyPipeline --> BatchAgg[Batch Aggregation]
    ListeningHistory[(Listening History)] --> RecEngine[Offline Recommendation Engine]
    RecEngine --> DiscoverWeekly[Precomputed Personalized Playlist]

title: Design a Podcast Platform

stages.prompt: Design a podcast platform that lets creators publish episodes (via RSS feed ingestion, the podcast industry standard) and listeners stream/download and track playback progress across devices.
stages.answer: Ingest podcast content by periodically polling creators' RSS feeds (the standard distribution mechanism in the podcast ecosystem, rather than a proprietary upload-only flow) for new episodes, storing episode metadata and audio file references; serve audio via CDN for streaming, and sync playback position per user per episode across devices (a small, frequently-updated record: user, episode, position, timestamp) so a listener can pause on one device and resume on another seamlessly.

stages.prompt: How do you efficiently check thousands of creators' RSS feeds for new episodes without constantly polling every feed at high frequency, most of which haven't changed?
stages.answer: Use conditional HTTP requests (If-Modified-Since / ETag headers) when polling feeds, so a feed that hasn't changed returns a cheap 304 Not Modified response rather than the full feed content, and adapt polling frequency per feed based on its historical publishing pattern (a daily show polled more frequently than a monthly one) rather than polling every feed at the same fixed interval regardless of how often it actually publishes.

stages.prompt: How do you support accurate download/listen analytics for creators, given podcast 'downloads' historically have significant ambiguity (a download isn't necessarily a full listen)?
stages.answer: Distinguish between different measurement events explicitly (a file download/stream request vs. actual playback progress reported by the client, which requires the client to report periodic playback position updates, not just the initial request) and be transparent with creators about what each reported metric actually measures, since industry-standard 'downloads' metrics are known to be an imperfect proxy for actual listens — providing richer, clearly-labeled data (like completion rate, derived from playback position tracking) where available is more useful to creators than only reporting the ambiguous legacy download count.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    RSSFeed[Creator RSS Feed] -->|conditional poll, adaptive frequency| Ingestion[Feed Ingestion Service]
    Ingestion --> EpisodeDB[(Episode Metadata)]
    Ingestion --> ObjectStore[(Audio Storage)]
    ObjectStore --> CDN[CDN]
    Listener[Listener] -->|stream| CDN
    Listener -->|playback position sync| PositionStore[(Cross-device Playback Position)]
    PlaybackEvents[Playback Progress Events] --> Analytics[(Creator Analytics)]

title: Design a Code Hosting and Collaboration Platform

stages.prompt: Design the core architecture for a code hosting platform (like GitHub) supporting Git repository storage, pull requests, and code review at scale.
stages.answer: Store Git repositories on a distributed storage layer (sharded across many storage nodes, since a single machine can't hold every repository, with routing logic directing requests for a given repo to the correct shard), exposing the standard Git protocol (push/pull/clone) over that storage. Pull requests and code review are modeled as metadata layered on top of the underlying Git data (tracking the diff between branches, review comments anchored to specific lines/commits, approval status) in a separate application database, rather than being part of Git itself.

stages.prompt: A small number of extremely large or high-traffic repositories (e.g., a huge open-source monorepo) create hotspots that could degrade performance for other repositories sharing infrastructure. How do you handle this?
stages.answer: Apply the same noisy-neighbor mitigation used elsewhere in shared multi-tenant infrastructure: per-repository resource limits/rate limiting on operations (clone bandwidth, API request rate) so one very active repository can't degrade service for others, and route or dedicate infrastructure for known especially large/high-traffic repositories separately from the general shared pool, similar to how a large SaaS tenant might get dedicated infrastructure.

stages.prompt: How do you support fast, efficient code search across potentially billions of files in millions of repositories?
stages.answer: Build and maintain a separate search index (similar to a full-text search engine's inverted index, adapted for code-specific needs like symbol-aware and syntax-aware search rather than pure keyword matching) that's updated incrementally as repositories change, rather than searching Git repository data directly on every query, since Git's storage format isn't optimized for search access patterns — this is a similar 'don't query the source-of-truth store directly for a fundamentally different access pattern' principle as maintaining a separate search index in front of any large primary datastore.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Push[git push] --> Router[Repo Router]
    Router --> ShardA[(Storage Shard A)]
    Router --> ShardB[(Storage Shard B)]
    PullRequest[Pull Request] --> ReviewDB[(Review Metadata DB)]
    ReviewDB -.->|references| ShardA
    ShardA -->|incremental update| SearchIndex[(Code Search Index)]
    LargeRepo[Very Large/Hot Repo] -.->|dedicated infra| DedicatedShard[(Dedicated Storage)]

title: Design a Package Registry (npm-style)

stages.prompt: Design a package registry (like npm) that lets developers publish versioned software packages and other developers/build tools install them, resolving dependency trees.
stages.answer: Store published package versions as immutable artifacts (once a specific version is published, it can never be silently changed, only deprecated — this immutability is critical since builds everywhere depend on a specific version behaving identically forever) in object storage, with a metadata service tracking package names, versions, and dependency declarations. Installing a package requires resolving its full dependency tree (recursively fetching each dependency's declared dependencies) into a consistent set of versions satisfying all version constraints, which client tooling typically does, querying the registry's metadata API.

stages.prompt: A popular package is downloaded millions of times per day by CI systems and developer machines worldwide. How do you serve this efficiently?
stages.answer: Since published package versions are immutable, they're perfectly cacheable — put a CDN in front of package downloads so the vast majority of requests for popular packages are served from edge cache rather than hitting origin storage on every single download, identical in principle to how a container registry caches immutable image layers.

stages.prompt: A malicious actor publishes a package with a name very similar to a popular package (typosquatting) or compromises a legitimate maintainer's account to publish a malicious version. How do you address supply-chain security concerns?
stages.answer: Combine several mitigations rather than relying on one: automated scanning of published packages for known malicious patterns, requiring multi-factor authentication for publishing (especially for high-download-count packages), providing provenance/signature verification so consumers can verify a package version actually came from the claimed source, and giving the platform a fast takedown mechanism for confirmed-malicious packages — supply-chain security for a package registry is an ongoing operational and product concern, not a one-time technical fix, given attackers continuously adapt their techniques.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Publish[Package Publish] -->|immutable| ArtifactStore[(Object Storage)]
    Publish --> MetadataDB[(Package Metadata + Dependencies)]
    Install[Package Install] --> Resolver[Dependency Resolver]
    Resolver --> MetadataDB
    Install -->|download| CDN[CDN]
    CDN -->|cache miss| ArtifactStore
    SecurityScanner[Security Scanner] -.->|scan on publish| Publish

title: Design a DNS System

stages.prompt: Design a DNS resolution system that translates domain names to IP addresses, explaining the hierarchical lookup process for a globally distributed service.
stages.answer: DNS resolution is hierarchical: a client's resolver queries a root nameserver (which knows where to find top-level-domain servers), then the relevant TLD nameserver (e.g., for .com, which knows where to find the authoritative nameserver for the specific domain), then the domain's authoritative nameserver, which returns the actual IP address (or other record) — each layer delegates to the next more specific layer rather than any single server needing to know every domain in existence.

stages.prompt: This multi-hop lookup process would be slow if performed fully for every single request. How is DNS made fast in practice?
stages.answer: Aggressive caching at every layer: resolvers cache results for the duration specified by each record's TTL, so repeated lookups for the same domain within that window are served instantly from cache without repeating the hierarchical lookup; ISPs and organizations run their own caching resolvers shared across many users, and most DNS records use TTLs long enough (minutes to hours) that the vast majority of real-world lookups are served from some layer of cache rather than a fresh full hierarchical resolution.

stages.prompt: How does DNS support directing users to the geographically nearest server for a global service, and what's the tradeoff of using a short TTL to enable fast failover?
stages.answer: GeoDNS returns different IP addresses for the same domain based on the requester's geographic location (determined from their resolver's IP), directing users to a nearby data center/CDN edge for lower latency. Short TTLs enable faster failover (a changed DNS record propagates to clients sooner) but increase the load on authoritative nameservers (since caches expire and re-query more often) and mean clients experience slightly more of the full resolution latency more frequently — this is a genuine tradeoff between failover speed and both server load and average lookup latency, and the right TTL depends on how much you prioritize each.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Client[Client Resolver] -->|cache miss| Root[Root Nameserver]
    Root --> TLD[TLD Nameserver - .com]
    TLD --> Authoritative[Authoritative Nameserver]
    Authoritative -->|GeoDNS: nearest IP| Client
    Client -->|cached, TTL-bound| Cache[(Resolver Cache)]
    CachingResolver[ISP Caching Resolver] -.->|shared cache| Client

title: Design a Global Load Balancing System

stages.prompt: Design a global load balancing system that routes users to the best available data center/region for a service operating in multiple regions worldwide.
stages.answer: Combine DNS-based geo-routing (directing users to a nearby region based on their resolver's location, as in GeoDNS) with health-aware routing (excluding a region from receiving new traffic if it's detected as unhealthy/overloaded) and, for finer-grained control than DNS TTLs allow, anycast routing at the network layer (announcing the same IP address from multiple locations, letting internet routing itself direct a user's traffic to the topologically nearest healthy location) — anycast provides faster failover than DNS-based approaches since it doesn't depend on DNS cache expiry.

stages.prompt: A region goes down entirely (e.g., a cloud provider outage). How does global traffic get rerouted away from it quickly?
stages.answer: Continuous health checking of each region (from multiple external vantage points, to avoid a single checker's own connectivity issue causing a false 'region down' determination) feeds into the routing layer's decision-making — with anycast, withdrawing the BGP route advertisement for the failed region from that location causes internet routing to naturally redirect traffic to the next-nearest healthy location within routing-protocol convergence time (typically fast, seconds to low minutes); with DNS-based routing alone, failover is bounded by DNS TTL, which is why anycast or a hybrid approach is preferred when very fast failover matters.

stages.prompt: How do you avoid overloading a healthy region by suddenly redirecting all of a failed region's traffic to it?
stages.answer: Global load balancing decisions should account for each remaining healthy region's current capacity/headroom, not just proximity — distributing failed-over traffic across multiple healthy regions proportional to their available capacity rather than dumping it all onto the single nearest one, which could turn one region's outage into a second region's overload if that region wasn't provisioned with enough spare capacity to absorb a neighboring region's full failover traffic.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    User[User] --> Anycast[Anycast IP / GeoDNS]
    Anycast -->|nearest healthy| RegionA[Region A]
    Anycast -.->|region A down, reroute| RegionB[Region B]
    Anycast -.-> RegionC[Region C]
    HealthChecks[Multi-vantage-point Health Checks] --> Anycast
    CapacityAware[Capacity-aware Failover Distribution] --> Anycast

title: Design a Multi-Region Active-Active Database

stages.prompt: Design a database architecture that accepts both reads and writes in multiple geographic regions simultaneously (active-active), for an application needing low write latency for users worldwide.
stages.answer: Each region runs a local database instance accepting writes, with changes replicated asynchronously to other regions — this gives every region fast local writes (no cross-region round-trip needed to commit), but means the system operates under eventual consistency between regions, since a write in one region takes some time to propagate to others, during which a read in a different region could see stale data.

stages.prompt: Two users in different regions concurrently update the same record before replication catches up. How do you resolve this conflict when the two regions' copies later sync?
stages.answer: Conflict resolution needs an explicit strategy since it can't be avoided entirely in active-active — common approaches include last-writer-wins (based on a synchronized timestamp, simple but can silently lose one update), a CRDT-based data model for fields where merges can be defined automatically and safely (as used in collaborative editors), or application-level conflict resolution (detecting the conflict and either merging semantically or surfacing it for manual/business-logic-driven resolution) — the right approach depends heavily on the specific data and how costly silently losing an update would be for that use case.

stages.prompt: For data where losing an update or having temporary inconsistency is genuinely unacceptable (e.g., a financial balance), how do you handle it within an otherwise active-active architecture?
stages.answer: Not all data needs to be active-active — for specific data requiring strong consistency, route those particular operations to a single authoritative region (accepting the latency cost of a cross-region write for just that data) rather than trying to force strong consistency guarantees onto the entire system's active-active model. This selective approach (active-active for most data, single-writer for specifically consistency-critical data) is a common and reasonable middle ground rather than an all-or-nothing architectural choice.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    UserA[User - Region A] -->|local write| DBA[(Region A DB)]
    UserB[User - Region B] -->|local write| DBB[(Region B DB)]
    DBA <-.->|async replication| DBB
    ConflictResolver[Conflict Resolution\nLWW / CRDT / app-level] -.-> DBA
    ConflictResolver -.-> DBB
    CriticalData[Consistency-critical Data] -->|routed to single region| AuthoritativeDB[(Authoritative Region)]

title: Design a GDPR / Data Deletion Compliance Pipeline

stages.prompt: Design a system that lets a company reliably fulfill a user's 'right to be forgotten' request (GDPR Article 17), deleting their personal data across all systems within the required timeframe.
stages.answer: The hard part isn't deleting from one database — it's that user data is typically scattered across many systems (primary databases, caches, search indexes, analytics warehouses, backups, third-party processors, log files). A deletion pipeline needs a data inventory/map (knowing every system that stores personal data for a given user) and orchestrates a deletion (or anonymization) request across all of them, tracking completion status per system so the request can be verified as fully complete, not just fired-and-hoped.

stages.prompt: Some data lives in systems that aren't designed for individual-record deletion (like immutable event logs, or backups that can't be selectively edited). How do you handle these?
stages.answer: For systems where true deletion isn't practical (like restoring from an old backup that would reintroduce deleted data), common accepted approaches include: ensuring backups have their own expiration/rotation policy so old backups containing the data age out naturally within a bounded time, and for logs/analytics data, replacing personal identifiers with an anonymized/pseudonymized token rather than deleting the whole record, satisfying the intent (the data is no longer personally identifiable) without needing surgical deletion from an append-only structure not built for it.

stages.prompt: How do you prove compliance (to regulators or auditors) that a deletion request was actually fully completed across every relevant system?
stages.answer: Maintain an auditable record of every deletion request's full lifecycle — which systems were identified as needing action, confirmation of completion from each, and a timestamp of when the overall request was fully satisfied — so compliance can be demonstrated with evidence rather than just an assertion. Treat an incomplete or stalled deletion request (a system that didn't confirm completion) as an alertable operational issue requiring follow-up, not something that silently falls through the cracks.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    Request[Deletion Request] --> DataMap[Personal Data Inventory/Map]
    DataMap --> PrimaryDB[(Primary DB - delete)]
    DataMap --> SearchIndex[(Search Index - delete)]
    DataMap --> Analytics[(Analytics Warehouse - anonymize)]
    DataMap --> Backups[(Backups - bounded expiry)]
    DataMap --> ThirdParty[Third-party Processors]
    PrimaryDB -->|confirm| AuditLog[(Deletion Audit Log)]
    SearchIndex -->|confirm| AuditLog
    AuditLog -->|incomplete| Alert[Alert: Stalled Deletion]

title: Design an Identity and Access Management (IAM) System

stages.prompt: Design an IAM system that manages user identities, roles, and permissions across many internal services and resources at a company.
stages.answer: Model access via role-based access control (RBAC): users are assigned roles, roles are granted permissions on resources, and an authorization check evaluates whether a user's roles grant the requested permission on the requested resource — centralizing this logic in an IAM service that other services call (or that issues tokens/claims embedding the relevant permissions) rather than each service independently implementing its own permission logic, which reliably leads to inconsistent enforcement.

stages.prompt: A large organization has thousands of fine-grained permissions and resources, and pure RBAC with a huge flat set of roles becomes unwieldy ('role explosion'). How do you address this?
stages.answer: Introduce hierarchy and composition: support role inheritance (a role can include other roles' permissions), and for genuinely fine-grained, contextual access needs, consider attribute-based access control (ABAC) as a complement to RBAC — where access decisions can depend on attributes of the user, resource, and context (e.g., 'engineers on team X can access resources tagged with team X'), which scales better than trying to enumerate an explicit role for every possible fine-grained access combination.

stages.prompt: How do you handle access review and de-provisioning — ensuring people don't accumulate excessive access over time (e.g., after changing teams) and that access is revoked promptly when someone leaves?
stages.answer: Implement periodic automated access reviews (surfacing each user's current roles/permissions to their manager or a resource owner for re-certification on a schedule, flagging unused or unusually broad access) rather than relying on access grants being manually cleaned up, since access naturally accumulates over time as people change roles and nobody proactively removes now-unneeded grants. Integrate de-provisioning directly with the company's HR/identity lifecycle system so an employee's departure automatically and immediately triggers access revocation across all integrated systems, rather than depending on a manual offboarding checklist step that can be missed.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    User[User] -->|assigned| Role[Role - RBAC]
    Role -->|grants| Permission[Permission on Resource]
    Service[Internal Service] -->|authz check| IAMService[IAM Service]
    IAMService --> Role
    HRSystem[HR/Identity Lifecycle] -.->|employee departs| Deprovision[Automatic De-provisioning]
    AccessReview[Periodic Access Review] -.->|flags stale access| Role

title: Design a Single Sign-On (SSO) System

stages.prompt: Design an SSO system that lets a user log in once and gain access to multiple separate applications without re-authenticating for each.
stages.answer: A central identity provider (IdP) handles authentication; when a user tries to access an application (service provider), they're redirected to the IdP to log in (if not already authenticated), and upon success, the IdP issues a signed token/assertion (using a standard protocol like SAML or OIDC) that the application verifies to establish the user's identity and grant access — subsequent applications the user visits in the same session can skip the login prompt entirely since the IdP recognizes the user already has an active session.

stages.prompt: How does the IdP recognize a returning user already has an active session, avoiding a repeated login prompt when they navigate to a second application?
