stages.answer: The IdP sets its own session cookie (scoped to the IdP's own domain) when the user first authenticates; when redirected back to the IdP for a second application, the browser sends this existing cookie, letting the IdP recognize the active session and skip straight to issuing a new token for the second application without prompting for credentials again — the user only re-authenticates once the IdP's own session expires or they explicitly log out.

stages.prompt: A user's account is compromised and needs to be locked out of all connected applications immediately. How does SSO make this easier (or harder) compared to each application managing its own separate login?
stages.answer: SSO is a significant security improvement here specifically: revoking the user's session/credentials at the central IdP immediately prevents new access to every connected application (since they all depend on the IdP for authentication), rather than needing to separately disable the account in every individual application's own user database — this centralization is one of SSO's biggest security benefits, though it also means the IdP itself becomes a very high-value target and single point of failure, so its own security needs to be exceptionally robust.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    User[User] -->|access App A| AppA[Application A]
    AppA -->|redirect if not authenticated| IdP[Identity Provider]
    IdP -->|login + session cookie| User
    IdP -->|signed token| AppA
    User -->|access App B| AppB[Application B]
    AppB -->|redirect| IdP
    IdP -->|existing session, no re-login| AppB
    Admin[Security Admin] -->|revoke| IdP

title: Design an API Key Management System

stages.prompt: Design a system that lets developers generate, manage, and use API keys to authenticate programmatic access to your platform's API.
stages.answer: On key generation, create a cryptographically random key, store only a hashed version server-side (never the raw key, following the same principle as password storage — the raw key is shown to the user once at creation time and never retrievable again), and associate the key with metadata (owner, scopes/permissions, creation date, expiration). Every API request presenting a key looks up the hash to identify the caller and enforce whatever permissions/rate limits are associated with that specific key.

stages.prompt: A developer accidentally commits an API key to a public GitHub repository. How does the system help detect and respond to this quickly?
stages.answer: Beyond the affected developer manually noticing and revoking it, proactively scan for the platform's own key patterns appearing in public code repositories (many major platforms partner with GitHub's secret-scanning program, or run their own scanning, specifically for this) and automatically revoke or flag leaked keys the moment they're detected in a public location, notifying the owner — this dramatically reduces the exposure window compared to relying solely on the developer noticing their own mistake.

stages.prompt: How do you support fine-grained permission scoping so a leaked key does limited damage, rather than every key having full account access?
stages.answer: Support scoped keys (a key can be restricted to specific permissions/endpoints/resources at creation time — read-only, specific API namespaces, specific resource IDs) rather than only offering all-or-nothing full-account keys, so developers can follow least-privilege practice and issue a narrowly-scoped key for each specific integration's actual needs — meaning a single leaked key exposes only what that key was scoped to, not the entire account.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Developer[Developer] -->|generate key| KeyService[Key Management Service]
    KeyService -->|hash only stored| KeyStore[(Key Store - hashed)]
    APIRequest[API Request + Key] --> AuthCheck[Auth + Scope Check]
    AuthCheck --> KeyStore
    GitHubScan[Public Repo Secret Scanning] -.->|leaked key detected| KeyService
    KeyService -->|auto-revoke + notify| Developer

title: Design a Web Application Firewall (WAF)

stages.prompt: Design a WAF that sits in front of web applications, inspecting incoming HTTP requests and blocking malicious traffic (SQL injection, XSS, common attack patterns) before it reaches the application.
stages.answer: Inspect each incoming request (headers, query parameters, body) against a set of rules — signature-based rules matching known attack patterns (e.g., SQL injection syntax patterns), and potentially anomaly-based detection (flagging requests that deviate significantly from normal traffic patterns for that application) — blocking or challenging (e.g., a CAPTCHA) requests that match, while passing legitimate traffic through with minimal added latency, since the WAF sits directly on the critical path of every request.

stages.prompt: A new rule incorrectly blocks legitimate traffic (a false positive), causing a production incident for a real customer. How do you prevent and quickly recover from this?
stages.answer: Support a 'detection/log-only mode' for new or modified rules before fully enabling blocking — running the rule against real traffic and logging what it *would* have blocked, letting engineers verify it doesn't false-positive on legitimate traffic before switching it to actively block. When a rule does cause a problem in production, support fast, targeted rollback of that specific rule (not just an all-or-nothing WAF disable) so unrelated protections stay active while the problematic rule is fixed.

stages.prompt: How does the WAF keep up with new, previously-unseen attack techniques, given a purely static signature-based ruleset will always lag behind novel attacks?
stages.answer: Combine static signature rules (fast, precise, but reactive — only catch known patterns) with anomaly/behavioral detection (catching unusual patterns even without a specific matching signature) and maintain a rapid rule-update pipeline (since new attack techniques and vulnerabilities are disclosed constantly, the WAF's ruleset needs to be a living, frequently-updated system, often informed by threat intelligence feeds) rather than treating the ruleset as something configured once and left static.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Request[Incoming HTTP Request] --> WAF[WAF]
    WAF -->|signature match| Block[Block/Challenge]
    WAF -->|anomaly detected| Flag[Flag/Challenge]
    WAF -->|clean| App[Application]
    NewRule[New Rule] -->|log-only mode first| WAF
    ThreatIntel[Threat Intelligence Feed] -.->|rule updates| WAF

title: Design a Polite Distributed Web Scraper

stages.prompt: Design a distributed web scraper that crawls and extracts structured data from many websites at scale, while respecting each site's crawling rules and not overwhelming any individual site.
stages.answer: This closely parallels general web crawler design: a URL frontier queue distributes work across many scraper workers, and per-domain rate limiting/politeness delays (respecting each site's robots.txt crawl-delay directive, or a sensible default) ensure no single site receives an overwhelming request rate regardless of how many workers the overall system runs, since aggregate scraper capacity is much larger than what any single target site should have to absorb.

stages.prompt: Many websites detect and block scraping via IP-based rate limiting or bot-detection. How do you scrape reliably (for legitimate, permitted use cases) without your scraper being blocked?
stages.answer: Respect the target site's stated policies (robots.txt, terms of service) as the starting point for what's permitted, and for legitimate scraping within those bounds, use a reasonable request rate and identify your scraper honestly via a proper User-Agent string rather than trying to evade detection — for scraping that requires higher volume, use a distributed pool of request sources (multiple IPs) specifically to stay within a *per-site* reasonable rate from any single source, not to circumvent a site's explicit rate limits, since the goal is being a well-behaved, unobtrusive client, not evading legitimate anti-abuse measures.

stages.prompt: How do you handle the extracted data varying wildly in structure across different websites, given each site's HTML layout is different?
stages.answer: Write site-specific extraction logic (parsers/selectors tailored to each target site's actual HTML structure) rather than trying to build one universal extractor that works everywhere, since website structures are too varied and change too unpredictably for a fully generic approach to be reliable — but centralize the surrounding infrastructure (the frontier queue, rate limiting, scheduling, storage) as shared, reusable components across all site-specific extractors, so adding a new target site means writing a new small parser, not rebuilding the whole pipeline.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Frontier[(URL Frontier - per domain)] --> Worker1[Scraper Worker]
    Frontier --> Worker2[Scraper Worker]
    Worker1 -->|robots.txt + rate limit per domain| TargetSite[Target Website]
    Worker1 --> SiteParser[Site-specific Parser]
    SiteParser --> ExtractedData[(Structured Data Store)]
    RobotsCheck[robots.txt / Politeness Check] -.-> Worker1

title: Design a Geo-Search Real Estate Listing Platform

stages.prompt: Design a real estate platform that lets users search for property listings within a geographic area (drawn on a map, or by radius from a point), combined with filters like price range and number of bedrooms.
stages.answer: Store each listing's location as coordinates, indexed using a geospatial indexing structure (like a geohash-based index or an R-tree) that supports efficient 'find all points within this region' queries, combined with standard filtering on structured attributes (price, bedrooms, property type) — geospatial queries and attribute filters typically both need to apply together, so the index/query engine needs to support combining them efficiently rather than doing a geospatial query and then filtering the (potentially huge) result set in application code.

stages.prompt: A popular metro area has tens of thousands of active listings, and search results need to render on a map without overwhelming the client with too many individual markers. How do you handle this?
stages.answer: Implement map clustering: when zoomed out (viewing a large area with many listings), group nearby listings into a single cluster marker showing a count, only rendering individual listing markers once the user zooms in enough that the number of listings in view drops to a manageable count — this is both a UX necessity (thousands of overlapping pins is unusable) and a performance necessity (the client shouldn't need to render or even receive thousands of individual markers for an overview-level map view).

stages.prompt: How do you keep search results fresh given listings are added, updated (price changes), and removed (sold/delisted) frequently, without stale listings (like already-sold properties) appearing in search results?
stages.answer: Update the geospatial/search index synchronously or near-synchronously with listing state changes (a sold/delisted property should disappear from active search results promptly, not linger for hours due to a batch reindex delay) since showing a user a listing that's no longer actually available is a poor experience that damages trust in the platform — this generally means an event-driven update to the index on every listing state change, rather than relying on periodic batch reindexing as the primary freshness mechanism.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Search[Search: region + filters] --> GeoIndex[(Geospatial Index)]
    GeoIndex -->|within region| Filter[Attribute Filters\nprice, bedrooms]
    Filter --> Results[Search Results]
    Results -->|zoomed out| Clustering[Map Clustering]
    ListingUpdate[Listing State Change] -->|near-synchronous| GeoIndex

title: Design a Ride-Hailing ETA Prediction System

stages.prompt: Design a system that predicts accurate estimated time of arrival (ETA) for a ride-hailing trip, both for driver-to-pickup and pickup-to-destination legs.
stages.answer: Combine a routing engine (computing the shortest/fastest path between two points over a road network graph) with a machine learning model that adjusts the raw routing-based time estimate based on real-world factors the graph alone doesn't capture — current traffic conditions, time of day/day of week patterns, weather, and historical actual-trip-time data for similar routes — since a naive distance/speed-limit-based estimate is often significantly wrong compared to real conditions.

stages.prompt: ETA predictions are consistently off in a specific city during certain hours (e.g., systematically underestimating trip time during school pickup/dropoff times). How do you detect and correct this kind of systematic bias?
stages.answer: Continuously compare predicted ETAs against actual observed trip times (readily available, since every completed trip provides ground truth) and monitor prediction error broken down by relevant dimensions (city, time of day, route type), which surfaces systematic biases like this one as a clear pattern in the error data rather than requiring someone to manually notice the issue — feed this error analysis back into model retraining, and for well-understood recurring patterns (a known local event causing regular congestion), consider explicit feature engineering (like a school-hours indicator for that specific area) rather than relying entirely on the model to infer it from raw historical data alone.

stages.prompt: How do you make ETA predictions update dynamically during an active trip as real conditions change (e.g., unexpected traffic building up)?
stages.answer: Continuously re-predict the remaining ETA during the trip using the driver's current live location and current real-time traffic conditions (not just the original prediction made at trip start), pushing updated ETAs to both rider and driver apps periodically — treating the initial ETA as a starting estimate that should be refined throughout the trip as better, more current information becomes available, rather than a single static prediction that goes stale as the trip progresses.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    TripRequest[Trip Request] --> RoutingEngine[Routing Engine]
    RoutingEngine -->|base route + time| MLAdjust[ML ETA Adjustment Model]
    TrafficData[Real-time Traffic] --> MLAdjust
    HistoricalTrips[(Historical Trip Data)] --> MLAdjust
    MLAdjust --> ETA[Predicted ETA]
    ActiveTrip[Active Trip - live location] -->|continuous re-prediction| MLAdjust
    CompletedTrips[(Completed Trip Outcomes)] -.->|error analysis, retraining| MLAdjust

title: Design an Inventory / Supply Chain Management System

stages.prompt: Design an inventory management system for a retailer with multiple warehouses, tracking stock levels accurately and supporting order fulfillment from the right warehouse.
stages.answer: Track inventory per SKU per warehouse as a core data model, with every inventory-affecting event (a sale, a warehouse transfer, a restock, a return) recorded as an atomic transaction against the specific warehouse's stock count — when an order comes in, a fulfillment routing decision picks the best warehouse to fulfill from (considering stock availability, proximity to the customer for shipping cost/speed, and current warehouse load) and reserves that inventory for the order.

stages.prompt: The system shows a SKU as in-stock at a warehouse, but a physical inventory count reveals a discrepancy (theft, damage, a recording error) — the digital record and physical reality have drifted apart. How do you handle and prevent this?
stages.answer: This kind of drift is somewhat inevitable over time in any physical inventory system, so support regular reconciliation processes (periodic physical cycle counts compared against system records, with discrepancies investigated and the system corrected) rather than assuming the digital record is always perfectly accurate. To reduce drift in the first place, ensure every physical inventory movement (receiving, picking, shipping, returns processing) has a corresponding system-of-record transaction at the point it happens (e.g., barcode scanning integrated into warehouse operations) rather than relying on manual, delayed, or batch updates that are more prone to being missed or recorded incorrectly.

stages.prompt: How do you handle demand forecasting to decide how much stock to hold and when to reorder, balancing the cost of excess inventory against the cost of stockouts?
stages.answer: Use historical sales data (accounting for seasonality, trends, and promotional effects) to forecast expected demand per SKU per warehouse over the relevant reorder lead time, and set reorder points/quantities based on that forecast plus a safety-stock buffer sized according to forecast uncertainty and the specific cost tradeoff for that product (a fast-moving low-margin item might tolerate a leaner buffer than a slow-moving high-margin one) — this is fundamentally a statistical forecasting and optimization problem layered on top of the core inventory tracking system, not something the tracking system alone solves.

diagram:
flowchart TD
    SaleEvent[Sale/Transfer/Restock Event] -->|atomic transaction| WarehouseStock[(Per-warehouse Stock by SKU)]
    Order[Incoming Order] --> FulfillmentRouter[Fulfillment Routing]
    FulfillmentRouter --> WarehouseStock
    FulfillmentRouter -->|reserve stock| BestWarehouse[Chosen Warehouse]
    CycleCount[Physical Cycle Count] -.->|reconciliation| WarehouseStock
    HistoricalSales[(Historical Sales Data)] --> ForecastEngine[Demand Forecast Engine]
    ForecastEngine -->|reorder point/quantity| WarehouseStock

title: Design a HIPAA-Compliant Healthcare Records System

stages.prompt: Design a system for storing and sharing electronic health records (EHR) between healthcare providers, meeting HIPAA requirements for protecting patient health information.
stages.answer: Encrypt patient health data both at rest and in transit, enforce strict role-based access control (only clinicians with an actual treatment relationship to a patient, or explicit authorization, can access their records — not blanket access for all staff), and log every single access to patient data (who accessed what record, when, and in what context) in an immutable audit trail, since HIPAA specifically requires the ability to account for disclosures and detect inappropriate access.

stages.prompt: A doctor needs emergency access to a patient's records in a situation where normal authorization workflows (like confirming an active treatment relationship) would be too slow. How do you handle this without either blocking legitimate emergency care or leaving a security hole?
stages.answer: Support a 'break-glass' emergency access mechanism: authorized emergency access bypasses normal restrictions but requires the accessing clinician to provide a reason, is heavily logged and flagged for mandatory subsequent review, and triggers an alert to compliance/security staff — this balances not blocking genuinely urgent patient care against ensuring emergency access provisions aren't quietly used as a routine workaround for normal access controls, since every break-glass access should be scrutinized after the fact even though it wasn't blocked in the moment.

stages.prompt: How do you support data sharing between different healthcare organizations (referrals, specialist consultations) while maintaining the same strict access controls and audit requirements?
stages.answer: Use standardized healthcare interoperability protocols (like HL7 FHIR) for structured data exchange between organizations, with explicit, auditable consent/authorization for each specific data-sharing event (a patient's data being shared with a new provider should be a deliberate, logged, ideally patient-consented action, not an open pipe between organizations), and ensure the receiving organization's own system is also held to equivalent security/audit standards, since a compliant sharing mechanism doesn't help if the data ends up in a poorly-secured system on the other end.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Clinician[Clinician] -->|RBAC + treatment relationship check| AccessControl[Access Control Layer]
    AccessControl --> EHR[(Encrypted Patient Records)]
    AccessControl -->|every access| AuditLog[(Immutable Audit Log)]
    Clinician -->|urgent, bypass| BreakGlass[Break-glass Emergency Access]
    BreakGlass -->|flagged for review| ComplianceTeam[Compliance Review]
    ProviderB[Other Healthcare Org] -->|FHIR, consented| DataSharing[Data Sharing Exchange]
    DataSharing --> EHR

title: Design an Online Code Execution / Judge System

stages.prompt: Design an online code judge system (like LeetCode's own execution backend) that accepts user-submitted code in multiple languages, runs it against test cases, and returns pass/fail results with execution time and memory usage.
stages.answer: On submission, queue the code for execution rather than running it synchronously in the request path (execution time varies and shouldn't block the web server), and a worker picks it up and executes it inside an isolated sandbox (container or microVM, no network access, strict CPU/memory/time limits) — never executing arbitrary user-submitted code directly on a shared host, for the same isolation reasons as an AI agent's code-execution sandbox. Run the code against each test case, capturing output, execution time, and memory usage, and compare actual output against expected output to determine pass/fail.

stages.prompt: A submission contains an infinite loop or attempts a fork-bomb-style resource exhaustion attack. How does the sandbox prevent this from affecting the platform?
stages.answer: Enforce hard, non-overridable resource limits at the container/VM level (CPU time limit, memory limit, process/thread count limit, wall-clock timeout) that forcibly terminate the sandboxed execution once exceeded, regardless of what the code inside attempts to do — this needs to be enforced by the isolation layer itself (not something the executed code could disable or exceed), since the whole point of the sandbox is protecting the platform from arbitrary, potentially malicious or simply buggy user code.

stages.prompt: How do you support many programming languages (each with different compilers/interpreters and startup overhead) while keeping execution fast and the system maintainable?
stages.answer: Maintain a set of pre-built, versioned execution images per supported language (with the compiler/interpreter and any standard libraries pre-installed), so spinning up a sandbox for a given language doesn't require installing anything at execution time — combined with a warm pool of ready sandboxes per language (similar to a serverless platform's warm-start optimization) to minimize the startup latency users experience when submitting code, especially important given users expect near-immediate feedback on a code submission.

diagram:
flowchart LR
    Submission[Code Submission] --> Queue[(Execution Queue)]
    Queue --> Worker[Judge Worker]
    Worker --> SandboxPool[Warm Sandbox Pool - per language]
    SandboxPool --> Sandbox[Isolated Sandbox\nresource-limited, no network]
    Sandbox -->|output, time, memory| Compare[Compare vs Expected Output]
    Compare --> Result[Pass/Fail Result]
    Sandbox -->|limits exceeded| Terminate[Forced Termination]
